bank: I.A.1
At a gear plant, heat-treated parts go straight from the heat-treat department to the grinding department. In quality terms, the grinding department is:
An internal customer of heat treat
An external customer, because it is a separate cost center
An internal supplier to the heat-treat department
A downstream stakeholder rather than a customer

Anyone inside the organization who receives the output of a process is an internal customer of that process. Being a separate cost center does not make grinding external; external customers sit outside the organization.
std
I.A.1
A contract molder makes plastic housings that a device maker assembles into blood glucose meters sold in pharmacies. Which of these is an external customer of the molder?
The molder's packing cell that boxes the housings
The molder's tool room that maintains the molds
The molder's resin supplier that ships the pellets
The person who buys and uses the finished meter

External customers are outside the organization and include both the direct buyer (the device maker) and the end user of the finished product. The packing cell and tool room are internal, and the resin supplier is a supplier, not a customer.
std
I.A.1
A new car buyer never mentions that the doors must keep rain out, yet a leaking door would make her very dissatisfied. This expectation is best described as:
A basic need the customer assumes will be met
A delighter that the customer does not expect at all
A performance need that rises with each added feature
A requirement the customer chose not to specify

Basic (must-be) expectations are so assumed that customers rarely state them, and meeting them earns no praise while missing them causes strong dissatisfaction. A delighter is unexpected and pleases when present; it does not cause anger when absent.
std
I.A.1
A service manager wants to know how satisfied customers are with field repairs. Which approach gives the most direct measure?
Count the formal complaints received each month
Track how many technicians are on each shift
Compare repair prices against two competitors
Survey a sample of recent repair customers

Asking customers directly, through a well-designed survey of a representative sample, measures satisfaction. Complaint counts are tempting but understate dissatisfaction, because most unhappy customers never complain and simply go elsewhere.
std
I.A.1
A survey of 400 customers uses a 1-to-5 scale. Results: 150 gave a 5, 110 gave a 4, 80 gave a 3, 40 gave a 2 and 20 gave a 1. What percentage are satisfied if satisfied means a rating of 4 or 5?
Ratings of 4 or 5 total 150 + 110 = 260, and 260 / 400 = 65%. Including the neutral 3s gives 85%, which overstates satisfaction; 37.5% counts only the 5s.
std
I.A.1
A final assembly team receives wiring harnesses from the plant's own harness cell, and some arrive mislabeled. The assembly team should treat the harness cell as:
An internal supplier whose output must meet agreed requirements
An external supplier covered by the purchasing contract
An internal customer whose needs assembly must satisfy
A support group that sits outside the customer-supplier chain entirely

The harness cell provides inputs to assembly inside the same organization, so it is an internal supplier and should be held to clear requirements just like an outside source. It is not an external supplier, because no purchase contract or outside company is involved.
std
I.A.1
A purchasing team wants a stronger long-term relationship with an outside supplier of castings. Which practice best supports this?
Rebid the part every quarter to keep pricing pressure high
Hold back forecasts so the supplier cannot plan a price rise
Limit contact to purchase orders, invoices and formal rejection notices
Share clear requirements, forecasts and regular performance feedback

Good supplier relations rest on clear requirements, open communication and regular feedback on performance. Frequent rebidding may cut price in the short term but discourages the supplier from investing in quality for the customer.
std
I.A.1
An external supplier's parts pass the supplier's own final inspection but are rejected at the customer's receiving inspection. What should the customer check first?
That both use the same drawing revision and gauge method
That the supplier has a valid ISO 9001 certificate on file
That the purchase price allows the supplier a fair margin
That receiving inspectors have increased their sample size

When two parties disagree on the same parts, the first suspects are different requirements (drawing revision) or different measurement methods. A valid certificate says nothing about why the two inspections disagree on these parts.
std
I.A.2
A carmaker adds heated seats to a model, while its paint shop works to cut the rate of paint runs. How do these two efforts relate to basic quality principles?
Heated seats are freedom from defects; fewer runs is a feature
Heated seats are a feature; fewer paint runs is freedom from defects
Both are features, because both make the car more attractive
Both are freedom from defects, because both of them please customers

Product features meet customer needs and drive sales, while freedom from defects (deficiencies) cuts failure, rework and dissatisfaction. Heated seats add a capability; fewer paint runs removes deficiencies, so the two are not the same kind of quality.
std
I.A.2
A garden hose meets every dimension and material callout on its drawing, but it kinks so easily in normal use that water stops flowing. Which quality principle does it fail?
Fitness for use
Conformance to the drawing
Freedom from manufacturing defects
Process monitoring and measuring

The hose conforms to its specification yet does not do what users need, so it fails fitness for use; the specification itself is inadequate. It is not a conformance failure, since every callout is met.
std
I.A.2
A plant shipped 4,000 brackets last month, and customers found 12 defective. What is the defective rate in parts per million (ppm)?
300 ppm
333 ppm
12 / 4,000 = 0.003, and 0.003 × 1,000,000 = 3,000 ppm. 333 comes from dividing the wrong way (4,000 / 12), and 300 or 30,000 come from misplacing the decimal.
std
I.A.2
Which statement best distinguishes process monitoring from process measuring?
Monitoring finds a value; measuring tracks status over time
Monitoring is done by operators; measuring only by the lab
Monitoring applies to products; measuring only to processes
Monitoring tracks status over time; measuring finds a value

Monitoring means checking the status of a process or product over time to see if it is behaving as expected, while measuring determines a quantity or value. Who does the work or what it is applied to does not define the difference.
std
I.A.2
A technician wants to know whether a filling machine drifts during a shift. Which approach is the best way to monitor it?
Weigh every container once the shift has ended and the line is down
Weigh a few containers at set intervals and plot them in order
Check the filler's set points once at startup and record them
Review customer weight complaints at the end of each month

Drift is a change over time, so samples must be taken at intervals during the run and kept in time order. Weighing everything at the end loses the time order, so a drift cannot be seen while it can still be corrected.
std
I.A.2
Before using a new set of thickness readings to judge whether a coating process is in tolerance, what should a technician confirm first?
That the readings average close to the nominal thickness
That the operator agrees the process has run normally
That the previous lot of coated parts was accepted
That the gauge is calibrated and suited to the tolerance

Conclusions from data are only as good as the measurement behind it, so the gauge must be calibrated and have adequate resolution for the tolerance. An average near nominal is tempting reassurance, but readings from a bad gauge can look fine and still be wrong.
std
I.A.2
A stamping process has produced no nonconforming parts for two quarters and all its features are well inside tolerance. Under the principle of continuous improvement, what is the best next step?
Keep seeking ways to cut variation, cost and waste
Stop monitoring, since the process has proved itself
Widen the tolerances to match the current output
Shift its inspection staff to the next new product

Continuous improvement means improving even processes that already meet requirements, for example by reducing variation or waste. Stopping monitoring removes the means of noticing if the process later changes.
std
I.A.2
A shaft diameter is specified as 12.50 ± 0.05 mm. Five shafts measure 12.46, 12.54, 12.56, 12.44 and 12.51 mm. How many of the five conform?
The limits are 12.45 to 12.55 mm. 12.46, 12.54 and 12.51 are inside; 12.56 is above the upper limit and 12.44 is below the lower limit, so 3 conform.
std
I.A.2
A work instruction requires a cure oven at 180 ± 5 °C for 20 to 25 minutes. A batch ran at 183 °C for 18 minutes. What should the technician conclude?
The batch conforms because the temperature was within limits
The batch did not meet the process specification
The batch conforms if the parts pass a visual check
The batch is acceptable, as the shortfall is under 10%
A process specification is met only when every parameter is within its limits; 18 minutes is below the 20-minute minimum. Being within the temperature limit does not make up for a short cure time.
std
I.A.2
What is the main purpose of the production part approval process (PPAP)?
To show the production process can consistently make conforming parts at the planned rate
To approve a part's design before the drawings are first released for quoting
To inspect every part in the first production lot before it is shipped
To certify the supplier's quality management system to a recognized international standard

PPAP gives evidence, from parts made with production tooling and processes, that the supplier understands all requirements and can meet them consistently at the quoted rate. It is not a design release, and it does not replace QMS certification.
std
I.A.2
A supplier has an approved PPAP for a machined housing. Which change would normally require the supplier to notify the customer and resubmit before shipping?
Replacing a worn cutting insert with an identical new one
Repainting the machine guards during a planned shutdown
Training a new operator on the existing job instructions
Moving the part's production to another plant

Relocating production changes the process conditions behind the approval, so PPAP expects notification and a new submission. Like-for-like insert replacement and routine training are normal process upkeep that the existing approval already covers.
std
I.A.3
Which statement correctly distinguishes a national standard from an international standard?
A national standard comes from one country's standards body; an international one from a multinational body such as ISO
A national standard is always required by law, while an international standard is always voluntary in every country
A national standard covers products only, while an international standard covers management systems only
A national standard is written by a single company, while an international standard is written by its trade customers

The difference is the issuing body and its reach: one country's standards body versus a multinational body such as ISO or IEC. Both kinds are normally voluntary unless a law or contract calls them up, so legal force is not the distinction.
std
I.A.3
A manufacturer sells into many countries and wants one quality management system standard that customers worldwide recognize. Which is the best fit?
The national military specification of its home country
The supplier quality manual of its largest customer
The product safety standard for its main product line
ISO 9001

ISO 9001 is the international QMS standard used and recognized across many countries. A national military specification or one customer's manual has a narrower reach, and a product standard does not define a management system.
std
I.A.3
What does a quality management system standard such as ISO 9001 mainly set out?
Dimensions and tolerances that each product must meet before shipping
Requirements for how an organization manages its work to meet customer needs
Step-by-step instructions that operators follow at each individual workstation
Prices, lead times and payment terms agreed with each customer

A QMS standard specifies requirements for the system: processes, responsibilities, control and improvement. Product dimensions belong in product specifications, and step-by-step instructions are the organization's own work instructions.
std
I.A.3
A purchase order includes a packaging rule that is stricter than the plant's standard packaging procedure. What should the plant do?
Follow its own procedure, since it is part of the certified QMS
Use whichever method costs less and note it on the packing slip
Meet the customer's packaging rule for that order
Ship as usual and ask the customer to approve it after delivery

Customer requirements stated in the order must be met; the plant's procedure is a baseline, not a reason to ignore a stricter contract term. Being part of a certified system does not override what the customer has specified.
std
I.A.3
Which of these is a process specification rather than a product specification?
Wave solder bath at 250 ± 5 °C
Shaft diameter of 10.00 ± 0.02 mm
Painted panel gloss of at least 85 units
Bolt tensile strength of at least 400 MPa

A process specification sets conditions for how the work is done, such as temperatures, speeds or times. Diameter, gloss and tensile strength are characteristics of the finished product, so they are product specifications.
std
I.A.3
A pin drawing states a surface hardness of 58 to 62 HRC, and a separate heat-treat procedure states furnace time and quench temperature. How are these best classed?
The hardness is a process specification; the furnace settings are a product specification
The hardness is a product specification; the furnace settings are a process specification
Both are product specifications, because both affect the finished pin
Both are QMS requirements, because both appear in controlled documents

Hardness is a property of the finished pin, so it is a product specification; furnace time and quench temperature control how the pin is made, so they are process specifications. Being in controlled documents does not turn them into QMS requirements.
std
I.A.3
A customer asks whether a supplier's ISO 9001 certificate alone guarantees that its parts meet the drawing. What is the best answer?
Yes; certification means every shipment has been checked against the drawing
Yes; the registrar audits each part number against its drawing before issuing the certificate
No; it shows a managed system, but parts must still be verified to the drawing
No; ISO 9001 applies only to service providers, not to manufacturers

ISO 9001 certification shows the supplier operates a quality management system meeting the standard, not that every part conforms. Registrars audit the system on a sample basis; they do not check each part number against its drawing.
std
I.A.4
Which of these is a prevention cost?
Inspecting incoming steel bar against the purchase order
Reworking welds found cracked before the parts leave
Paying freight on a shipment the customer returned
Training operators on a new method before launch

Prevention costs are spent to stop defects from happening, such as training, planning and process design. Incoming inspection is tempting because it is done early, but it is appraisal: it checks for defects rather than preventing them.
std
I.A.4
In a cost of quality system, the cost of calibrating the plant's inspection gauges is classified as:
Appraisal
Prevention
Internal failure
External failure

Calibration keeps inspection and test equipment accurate, so it is part of the cost of evaluating product, which is appraisal. Some see it as prevention, but it supports measurement rather than preventing defects in the process.
std
I.A.4
Parts with a defect are caught at the plant's final inspection and scrapped. If missed, the same defect would have led to warranty claims. How are the two costs classified?
Scrap is appraisal cost; warranty is internal failure cost
Scrap is internal failure; warranty is appraisal
Scrap is internal failure; warranty is external failure
Scrap is external failure; warranty is prevention

Failure costs found before the product reaches the customer are internal; those found after delivery are external. The inspection itself is appraisal, but the scrap it produces is an internal failure cost.
std
I.A.4
Which of these is an external failure cost?
Re-inspecting a lot after in-house rework of a bad batch
Field service labor to replace a unit under warranty
Supplier quality planning for a part that is coming soon
Scrapping parts after a setup error at the first station
External failure costs arise after the product reaches the customer, such as warranty repairs, returns and field service. Re-inspection after rework happens inside the plant, so it is not external.
std
I.A.4

A plant's annual quality-related costs include operator training $12,000, incoming inspection $30,000, scrap $25,000, warranty repairs $40,000 and gauge calibration $8,000. What is the total appraisal cost?
Appraisal covers incoming inspection ($30,000) and gauge calibration ($8,000), for $38,000. Adding training gives $50,000, but training is prevention; scrap and warranty are failure costs.
std
I.A.4
A company reports prevention $20,000, appraisal $45,000, internal failure $80,000 and external failure $55,000. Using the common definition, what is its cost of poor quality (COPQ)?
COPQ in its common form is the failure costs: $80,000 + $55,000 = $135,000. $200,000 is the total cost of quality, which also includes prevention and appraisal.
std
I.A.4
A firm has prevention $15,000, appraisal $35,000, internal failure $60,000 and external failure $90,000, on annual sales of $5,000,000. What is total cost of quality as a percentage of sales?
Total COQ is $15,000 + $35,000 + $60,000 + $90,000 = $200,000, and $200,000 / $5,000,000 = 4.0%. Using only the failure costs gives 3.0%, which is COPQ, not total COQ.
std
I.A.4
A plant adds $15,000 a year in prevention. As a result, internal failure drops by $40,000 and external failure by $10,000, with appraisal unchanged. What is the effect on total cost of quality?
It falls by $50,000
It rises by $15,000
It falls by $65,000
It falls by $35,000
The change is +$15,000 − $40,000 − $10,000 = −$35,000. Counting only the failure savings gives $50,000, which ignores the added prevention spending.
std
I.A.4
A plant's cost of quality is 70% failure costs, 25% appraisal and 5% prevention. Where is the best opportunity to reduce total cost of quality over time?
Invest more in prevention to remove causes of failure
Add a final inspection step to catch defects before shipping
Cut prevention further, since it is already a small share
Shift warranty costs into the plant's scrap budget lines

Prevention addresses the causes of the failures that dominate this plant's costs, so it usually lowers total COQ. Extra final inspection raises appraisal and only moves some external failures to internal failures.
std
I.B.1
A team has a clear problem statement, "seal leaks on model 40 valves," and wants to list and organize every possible cause before collecting data. Which tool fits best?
Pareto chart
Scatter diagram
Control chart
Cause and effect diagram
A cause and effect diagram is built to brainstorm and group possible causes of a defined effect. A Pareto chart ranks categories that already have data; it does not generate the list of causes.
std
I.B.1
When constructing a cause and effect diagram, what is written at the head of the fish?
The cause the team thinks is most likely
A specific statement of the problem or effect
The corrective action the team has already chosen
The main category names used for the bones
The head holds the effect being studied, stated specifically, and the bones hold the possible causes. Putting the suspected cause at the head prejudges the analysis the diagram is meant to support.
std
I.B.1
Which set of main branches is commonly used on a cause and effect diagram for a manufacturing problem?
Plan, do, check and act, plus define and control
Sort, set in order, shine, standardize and sustain
People, machines, methods, materials, measurement and environment
Prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure costs

The common "6M" categories (people, machines, methods, materials, measurement and environment) help a team think broadly about causes. The other lists are PDCA and DMAIC steps, the 5S steps and the cost of quality categories.
std
I.B.1
A team's completed fishbone diagram lists 40 possible causes of a coating defect. What is the best next step?
Pick the likeliest causes and test them with data
Fix the causes that got the most votes right away
Treat every listed cause as a confirmed root cause
Add more branches until no idea is left unlisted

A fishbone shows possible causes, not proven ones, so the likeliest should be tested with data before action. Acting on votes alone risks fixing the wrong thing and spending money without solving the problem.
std
I.B.2
A team wants to see every step, decision and handoff in an order-entry process to find where orders are delayed. Which tool fits best?
Histogram
Flowchart
Scatter diagram
Check sheet
A flowchart shows the sequence of steps, decisions and handoffs, which is where delays and loops become visible. A check sheet could count delays later, but it does not show how the process flows.
std
I.B.2
In a standard flowchart, what does a diamond-shaped symbol represent?
The start or end point of the process
An operation step that transforms or changes the item
A decision point with two or more exit paths
A stored document or record of the work
A diamond marks a decision, such as accept or reject, with separate exit paths. Start and end points use rounded shapes (terminators), and activities use rectangles.
std
I.B.2
A team is mapping the current state of a receiving process. How should it build the flowchart?
Draw the process as the written procedure says it should be done
Draw the process as the team would like it to be done in future
Draw only the steps that add value and leave out the handoffs
Draw the process as it is actually done, confirmed by walking it
A current-state map must show reality, including workarounds and loops, so it should be checked on the floor. Copying the procedure is tempting but often hides the very steps that cause the problems.
std
I.B.2
A flowchart of a returns process shows parts looping back to "re-inspect" up to three times before they ship. What does this most likely indicate?
Rework loops that add time and cost but no value
A well-controlled process with strong built-in checks
A process that needs a second inspector at each step
A reporting error, because flowcharts cannot have loops

Repeated loops back to inspection point to rework and non-value-added effort, and they are a prime target for improvement. Repeated inspection is not good control; it signals that the earlier steps are not producing good output.
std
I.B.3
An inspector wants a quick way to record where on a molded panel scratches occur so the team can look for a pattern. Which tool fits best?
A Pareto chart of scratch counts by shift
A scatter diagram of scratch count by time
A location check sheet showing the panel
A histogram of scratch lengths in millimeters

A location (defect concentration) check sheet lets the inspector mark each defect on a picture of the part, so clusters show up directly. A Pareto chart ranks categories but does not show where on the part the defects are.
std
I.B.3
Before a team starts using a new check sheet for defect types, what should be settled first?
The improvement target that the collected data are expected to confirm
Clear definitions of each category and of the collection period
A list of the operators most likely to cause the defects
The chart type that will be used to show the final results
A check sheet gives useful data only if every collector classifies items the same way over a defined period. Setting the expected result first invites biased recording.
std
I.B.3
A check sheet records defects and parts produced by shift: first shift 14 defects in 1,400 parts, second shift 22 in 2,000 and third shift 44 in 5,500. Which shift has the lowest defect rate?
First, at 10 per 1,000 parts
Second, at 11 per 1,000 parts
First, with only 14 defects
Third, at 8 per 1,000 parts

The rates are 14/1,400 = 10, 22/2,000 = 11 and 44/5,500 = 8 per 1,000 parts, so third shift is lowest. First shift has the fewest defects, but raw counts mislead when the shifts make different numbers of parts.
std
I.B.4
A supervisor has a month of defect counts in 12 categories and wants to show which few categories account for most of the defects. Which tool fits best?
Pareto chart
Flowchart
Scatter diagram
Control chart

A Pareto chart ranks categories from largest to smallest with a cumulative line, which separates the vital few from the trivial many. A control chart shows change over time, not the ranking of categories.
std
I.B.4
Defect counts for a month are: scratches 72, dents 45, misalignment 18, wrong label 9 and other 6. On a Pareto chart, what cumulative percentage do the two largest categories reach?
The total is 150, and (72 + 45) / 150 = 117 / 150 = 78%. 48% is scratches alone, and 90% adds misalignment as a third category.
std
I.B.4
When constructing a Pareto chart, how should the bars be arranged?
Smallest to largest, so the main problem sits at the right
In the order that the defects occur along the process
Alphabetically, so readers can find each category quickly
Largest to smallest, with any "other" group placed last
Bars go in descending order of count or cost, with a catch-all "other" bar at the end even if it is larger than some categories. Process order belongs on a flowchart, not a Pareto chart.
std
I.B.4

A sample of 36 parts has x̄ = 25.40 mm. The process standard deviation is known to be 0.30 mm. Using z = 1.96, what are the 95% confidence limits for the mean?
The margin is 1.96 × 0.30 / √36 = 0.098, giving 25.30 to 25.50 mm. Leaving out √n gives 24.81 to 25.99 mm, and 25.32 to 25.48 mm uses the 90% value of 1.645.
std
II.B.3
An analyst rebuilds a confidence interval from the same data, changing the confidence level from 90% to 99%. What happens to the interval?
It becomes narrower
It becomes wider
It keeps the same width
It shifts toward the mean
A higher confidence level uses a larger z (or t) value, so the interval must be wider to give more assurance of capturing the true mean. The center stays at the sample mean.
std
II.B.3
A technician wants the confidence interval for a mean to be half as wide, at the same confidence level. Assuming the standard deviation stays the same, how should the sample size change?
Increase it about two times
Reduce it by about one half
Increase it about eight times
Increase it about four times
Interval width is proportional to 1/√n, so halving the width needs √n to double, which means n must quadruple. Doubling n only narrows the interval by about 29%.
std
II.B.3
A report gives the mean diameter as 10.03 mm with 95% confidence limits of 10.01 mm and 10.05 mm. A technician says this shows 95% of parts measure between 10.01 and 10.05 mm. Is she right?
Yes; the limits describe where 95% of the parts will measure
No; the limits show where 5% of the parts fall outside the spec
Yes; confidence limits and tolerance limits mean the same thing
No; the limits bound the mean, not individual parts

A confidence interval for the mean estimates where the true average lies; individual parts spread much wider than that. Treating the limits as a range for individual units confuses confidence limits with tolerance limits.
std
II.B.3
A technician builds a 95% confidence interval for a mean from only 8 measurements, and the population standard deviation is unknown. What should he use?
The z value of 1.96, with s used in place of σ
A t distribution with 7 degrees of freedom
A t distribution with 8 degrees of freedom
The z value of 1.645, since the sample is small

With σ unknown and a small sample, the t distribution with n − 1 = 7 degrees of freedom applies, giving a wider interval that reflects the uncertainty in s. Using z = 1.96 with s makes the interval too narrow.
std
II.C.1
How are the control limits on a control chart set?
Taken from the customer drawing tolerance so that the chart matches the print
Set at 75% of the specification width to give operators an early warning
Calculated from process data, usually at ±3 standard errors of the plotted statistic
Agreed with the customer in the control plan as the point at which parts are rejected

Control limits are the voice of the process, calculated from the process's own data. Limits copied from the tolerance, or set as a fraction of it, are based on specifications and say nothing about whether the process is stable.
std
II.C.1
Which statement best describes specification limits?
They state what the design or customer requires of the product
They are calculated from 20 to 25 subgroups taken while the process runs normally
They mark the range within which a stable process's subgroup averages will fall
They are recalculated whenever the process average shifts in a lasting way
Specification limits are the voice of the customer, set by design requirements. The other options describe control limits, which come from and change with process data.
std
II.C.1
An X̄ chart shows no points outside the limits and no unusual patterns, yet 4% of individual parts measure outside the specification. What is the right conclusion?
The process is stable but not capable, so the process itself must be changed
The process is out of control, so the operators should hunt for a special cause
The control limits are wrong and should be reset to match the specification
No action is needed, because the chart shows the process is in control

In control means stable and predictable, not that it meets the specification. Here it predictably makes 4% scrap, so reducing common cause variation or re-centering needs a change to the process; searching for a special cause will find nothing.
std
II.C.1
A supervisor asks that the specification limits be drawn on the X̄ chart so operators can see how close they are. Why is this a poor idea?
Specification limits are usually narrower than the control limits on an X̄ chart
Specification limits change with every subgroup, so they cannot be drawn as fixed lines
Specification limits apply to individual parts, but the chart plots subgroup averages
Specification limits are confidential and should not be shown to production staff

Averages vary less than individual values, so an average can sit well inside the specification while individual parts in that subgroup fall outside it. Mixing the two kinds of limits on one chart invites that false comfort.
std
II.C.1
On an X̄ chart, one subgroup average falls above the upper control limit, but every part in the subgroup is within specification. What should the operator do?
Continue running, since every part in the subgroup meets the specification
Look for a special cause, even though the parts conform
Scrap the subgroup, since a point above the limit means the parts are bad
Widen the control limits so that they match the specification limits

A point beyond a control limit signals that the process has changed, whether or not parts are yet out of specification; finding the cause now prevents later defects. Conforming parts do not mean the process is unchanged.
std
II.C.2
An X̄–R chart uses subgroups of n = 5. The grand average is 20.00 mm and R̄ is 0.50 mm. Using A2 = 0.577, what are the control limits for the X̄ chart?
20.64 mm and 19.36 mm
21.06 mm and 18.94 mm
20.13 mm and 19.87 mm
20.29 mm and 19.71 mm
UCL and LCL = X̿ ± A2R̄ = 20.00 ± 0.577 × 0.50 = 20.29 and 19.71 mm. 20.64 and 19.36 are ±3R̄/d2, the limits for individuals, which leave out the √n that A2 already includes.
std
II.C.2
For the same X̄–R chart (n = 5, R̄ = 0.50 mm), D3 = 0 and D4 = 2.114. What are the limits for the R chart?
UCL 1.057 mm, LCL −0.057 mm
UCL 0.789 mm, LCL 0.211 mm
UCL 1.141 mm, LCL 0
UCL 1.057 mm, LCL 0
UCL = D4R̄ = 2.114 × 0.50 = 1.057 mm and LCL = D3R̄ = 0. A range can never be negative, so a symmetric lower limit below zero is wrong, and 1.141 uses D4 for n = 4.
std
II.C.2
An individuals chart has an average of 50.0 and an average moving range (n = 2) of 1.2. Using E2 = 2.66, what are the limits for the individuals chart?
Limits are X̄ ± E2 × MR̄ = 50.0 ± 2.66 × 1.2 = 53.19 and 46.81. Using MR̄ directly as σ gives 53.60 and 46.40, and 52.26 and 47.74 use the X̄-chart factor A2 = 1.880 by mistake.
std
II.C.2
A batch chemical process yields one assay result per batch, and only a few batches are made each week. Which control chart fits best?
X̄–R chart with subgroups of five batches
p chart of the batches outside specification
Individuals and moving range (I-MR) chart
c chart of the defects found in each batch
With one measurement per batch and slow production, there is no natural subgroup, so an I-MR chart is used. Waiting for five batches to form a subgroup would delay signals for weeks.
std
II.C.2
A high-speed line gauges 15 caps every half hour for a variables characteristic. Which chart is most appropriate?
X̄–s chart
X̄–R chart
I-MR chart
np chart
For large subgroups, about ten or more, the standard deviation uses all the data and estimates spread better than the range, so X̄–s is preferred. X̄–R is the usual choice for small subgroups.
std
II.C.2
An X̄–s chart uses subgroups of n = 5. The grand average is 8.00 and s̄ is 0.20. Using A3 = 1.427, what are the X̄ chart limits?
Limits are X̿ ± A3s̄ = 8.00 ± 1.427 × 0.20 = 8.29 and 7.71. Using 3s̄/√n without the c4 correction gives 8.27 and 7.73, and 8.60 and 7.40 leave out √n altogether.
std
II.C.2
A new X̄–R chart is being set up. The R chart shows two points above its upper limit with known causes that were not removed. What should be done before using the X̄ chart?
Use the X̄ chart as it is, since only the R chart shows the problem
Raise the R chart limits until the two points fall inside them
Stabilize the ranges first; the X̄ limits are built from R̄
Switch to an X̄–s chart, which is not affected by unstable spread
The X̄ limits are X̿ ± A2R̄, so if the ranges are not in control the X̄ limits are unreliable. The spread must be stable first; switching to an X̄–s chart does not solve an unstable process.
std
II.C.2
When first calculating trial control limits for a variables chart, what data should be collected?
About 5 subgroups taken just after the most recent adjustment
About 20 to 25 subgroups taken while the process runs as normal
About 25 individual parts taken from the final inspection reject bin
About 100 subgroups taken only from the shift with the best results
Trial limits need enough subgroups, typically 20 to 25, collected under normal running conditions so they reflect the real process. Picking the best shift or reject parts biases the limits.
std
II.C.3
Each day a different-sized lot of circuit boards is tested, and each board is recorded as pass or fail. Which chart tracks the fraction of failing boards?
np chart
c chart
u chart
p chart
A p chart plots the proportion of defective units and handles changing sample sizes. An np chart plots the count of defectives and needs a constant sample size.
std
II.C.3
An inspector checks exactly 200 valves from every shift and counts the valves that leak. The team wants to chart the number of leaking valves directly. Which chart fits?
p chart
c chart
u chart
np chart
With a constant sample size and a count of defective units, the np chart plots the number defective directly. A p chart would also work but plots the proportion, not the count the team asked for.
std
II.C.3
An inspector counts paint blemishes on each car door, and all doors are the same size. Which chart is most suitable?
u chart
c chart
p chart
np chart
Blemishes are defects (one door can have several) counted on a constant area of opportunity, which is what a c chart is for. A u chart is needed only when the inspection area varies.
std
II.C.3
Fabric rolls of different lengths are inspected, and every flaw is counted. Which chart should track the flaw rate?
c chart
np chart
u chart
p chart
Flaws are defects, and the area inspected changes from roll to roll, so defects per unit (u) is plotted. A c chart assumes the same area of opportunity each time.
std
II.C.3
A p chart uses samples of n = 150, and the average fraction defective is 0.04. What are the control limits?
UCL 0.088, LCL 0
UCL 0.628, LCL 0
3√(0.04 × 0.96 / 150) = 0.048, so UCL = 0.088; the lower value of −0.008 is set to 0 because a proportion cannot be negative. 0.628 comes from leaving n out of the formula.
std
II.C.3
A c chart for defects per casting has c̄ = 9. The latest casting has 16 defects. How should this point be read?
It is inside the limits, so this point alone shows no special cause
It is above the UCL of 12, so a special cause should be investigated
It is above the UCL of 15, so a special cause should be investigated
It is inside the limits, so the process is now capable
c chart limits are c̄ ± 3√c̄ = 9 ± 9, giving a UCL of 18, so 16 is within the limits. A UCL of 12 adds only √c̄ once, and being in control says nothing about capability.
std
II.C.4
A team plans a capability study on a new turning operation. What should be confirmed first?
All parts in the study measure within the specification limits
A prior study on a similar machine showed a Cpk above 1.33
The process is stable, so its output is predictable
Unusual readings have been removed from the data set first

Capability indices predict future performance only if the process is stable; an unstable process has no single capability. Deleting unusual readings hides exactly the special causes the study needs to reveal.
std
II.C.4
Before reporting a Cpk, an engineer finds the gauge used for the study has a %GRR of 45% of the tolerance. What is the main concern?
Gauge error makes the process look more capable than it really is
Gauge error inflates the observed spread, so Cpk is unreliable
The Cpk is fine as long as the process is in statistical control
The study is fine because gauge error affects only Cp and not Cpk

An adequate measurement system is a prerequisite: measurement variation adds to the observed spread, so the reported index reflects the gauge as much as the process. It usually makes the process look worse, not better.
std
II.C.4
A shaft has specification limits of 9.70 mm and 10.30 mm. The process is stable with a standard deviation of 0.08 mm. What is Cp?
Cp = (USL − LSL) / 6σ = 0.60 / 0.48 = 1.25. Dividing by 3σ instead of 6σ gives 2.50, and 0.80 inverts the ratio.
std
II.C.4
The same shaft (limits 9.70 and 10.30 mm, σ = 0.08 mm) now runs with a mean of 10.10 mm. What is Cpk?
Cpk is the smaller of (10.30 − 10.10) / 0.24 = 0.83 and (10.10 − 9.70) / 0.24 = 1.67, so 0.83. Taking the larger side ignores the limit the process is closest to.
std
II.C.4
What is the key difference between Cp/Cpk and Pp/Ppk?
Cp and Cpk use overall σ from all data; Pp and Ppk use within-subgroup σ
Cp and Cpk use within-subgroup σ; Pp and Ppk use overall σ from all data
Cp and Cpk apply to variables data; Pp and Ppk apply to attributes data
Cp and Cpk need normal data; Pp and Ppk need no assumption about shape

Cp and Cpk use short-term, within-subgroup variation (for example R̄/d2), while Pp and Ppk use the overall standard deviation, which includes shifts between subgroups. Reversing the two is the most common mix-up.
std
II.C.4
An X̄–R study (n = 5) gives R̄ = 0.0465 mm, and the overall standard deviation of all readings is 0.025 mm. The tolerance width is 0.15 mm. Using d2 = 2.326, what is Pp?
Pp uses the overall σ: 0.15 / (6 × 0.025) = 1.00. Using the within-subgroup σ of R̄/d2 = 0.020 gives 1.25, which is Cp, not Pp.
std
II.C.4
A part has a specification of 25.00 ± 0.20 mm. The process mean is 25.08 mm and the overall standard deviation is 0.05 mm. What is Ppk?
std
II.C.4
A process shows Cp = 1.8 and Cpk = 0.9. What does this most likely indicate?
The spread is small enough, but the process is off center
The spread is too wide, so the process needs less variation
The process is centered but unstable from one shift to the next
The gauge is too coarse to measure the process properly
A high Cp means the spread fits well within the tolerance; a much lower Cpk means the mean sits close to one limit. Re-centering the process would raise Cpk toward 1.8 without reducing variation.
std
II.C.4
A process shows Cpk = 1.45 but Ppk = 0.90. What is the most likely explanation?
The within-subgroup spread is larger than the variation over the long term
The specification limits were changed between the two calculations
The mean shifts between subgroups over time, adding to the overall spread
The process is centered, so the two indices should not be compared

Ppk uses the overall standard deviation, which picks up drift and shifts between subgroups that Cpk's within-subgroup σ does not see. A large gap points to that between-subgroup variation; the within-subgroup spread is the smaller one.
std
II.C.4
A normally distributed, stable process has Cpk = 1.00. What does this mean for the specification limit closest to the mean?
It sits 6σ from the mean, so almost nothing falls beyond it
It sits 3σ from the mean, so about 0.135% falls beyond it
It sits 1σ from the mean, so about 16% falls beyond it
It sits 3σ from the mean, so about 0.27% falls beyond it
Cpk = 1.00 means the nearer limit is 3σ from the mean, and one tail beyond 3σ holds about 0.135% (1,350 ppm). 0.27% is the total for both tails, which applies only when both limits are 3σ away.
std
II.C.5
A stable process makes too many parts close to the upper specification limit. The chart shows no points outside the control limits and no patterns. Who is most likely able to fix this, and how?
The operator, by adjusting the machine after each high reading
The operator, by finding and removing the cause of the last high point
The inspector, by tightening the sampling plan at final inspection
Management, by changing the process, such as the equipment or method

With no signals, the variation is common cause, built into the system, so only a change to the system, usually directed by management, will reduce it. Chasing individual high readings treats common cause as special cause.
std
II.C.5
On a stable process, an operator adjusts the machine after every reading that is above or below target. What is the most likely result?
The process variation decreases
The process mean moves to target
The control limits get narrower
The process variation increases
Adjusting a stable process in response to common cause variation (tampering or overadjustment) adds the adjustments to the natural variation, so spread increases. It does not improve centering.
std
II.C.5
Just after a new lot of resin is loaded, an X̄ chart point falls above the upper control limit. What type of variation is indicated, and what should be done?
Common cause; leave the process alone and keep plotting the data
Special cause; find what changed, such as the resin, and correct it
Special cause; recalculate the control limits to include this point
Common cause; ask management to redesign the molding process
A point beyond a limit after a specific change signals special cause variation, which should be traced to its source and removed. Recalculating the limits to include it would hide the signal.
std
II.C.5
On an X̄ chart, nine consecutive points fall above the centerline, all within the control limits. How should this be interpreted?
As common cause variation, since all points fall inside the limits
As a sign that the limits are too wide and need to be tightened
As a special cause signal, suggesting the process mean has shifted
As expected behavior, since half of points fall above the centerline

A run of nine points on one side of the centerline is very unlikely if the process is unchanged, so it is a standard signal of a shift. Staying inside the control limits does not rule out a special cause.
std
II.C.5
An X̄ chart shows seven consecutive points each higher than the one before. What does this pattern most likely suggest?
A trend, such as gradual tool wear
A cycle, such as a daily heat change
A mixture of two separate streams
Normal variation inside the limits
Points rising steadily form a trend, which typically comes from something that changes gradually, such as tool wear or fixture loosening. A cycle repeats up and down rather than moving one way.
std
II.C.5
Fifteen consecutive X̄ chart points fall within one standard deviation of the centerline. What should be checked first?
Whether subgroups mix streams or the limits are old
Whether the process mean has shifted upward or downward
Whether the operators have started adjusting the machine more often
Whether the gauge reading has started to drift over time

Points hugging the centerline (stratification) often mean each subgroup combines several streams, inflating R̄, or that the limits were set before an improvement. A mean shift would push points to one side, not toward the center.
std
II.C.5
An X̄ chart's readings rise and fall in a repeating pattern that matches each shift change. What does this pattern indicate?
A trend caused by steady wear in the tooling over time
Stratification caused by subgroups that mix several streams
A cycle tied to something that changes each shift
Common cause variation that needs no investigation
A repeating up and down pattern is a cycle, which points to a factor that repeats on that schedule, such as operator rotation or temperature. A trend moves steadily in one direction.
std
II.C.5
An X̄ chart has a centerline of 50 and an upper control limit of 56 (σx̄ = 2). The last three points are 54.5, 51.0 and 54.8. Does this signal a special cause?
No; every one of the three points is inside the control limits
Yes; two of three consecutive points are beyond 2σ on one side
Yes; any point beyond 1σ from the centerline is a signal
No; the rule needs all three points to be beyond 2σ

The 2σ line is at 54, and 54.5 and 54.8 are two of three consecutive points beyond it on the same side, a common rule for lack of control. Being inside the 3σ limits does not rule out a signal from the zone rules.
std
III.A.1
A metric outside micrometer reads to 0.01 mm. On the sleeve, the 7 mm line and the 0.5 mm line just past it are exposed, and the thimble's 22 line aligns with the index line. What is the reading?
Sleeve 7.5 mm plus thimble 22 × 0.01 mm = 0.22 mm gives 7.72 mm. Reading 7.22 mm forgets the exposed half-millimeter line, the most common micrometer reading error.
std
III.A.1

On a vernier caliper with 0.02 mm resolution, the vernier zero sits just past the 23 mm main scale line, and the 17th vernier division counted from zero lines up best with a main scale line. What is the reading?
Each vernier division is worth 0.02 mm, so 17 × 0.02 = 0.34 mm, added to 23 mm gives 23.34 mm. Reading 23.17 mm treats each division as 0.01 mm, which is wrong for a 0.02 mm vernier.
std
III.A.1

A plunger dial indicator is graduated in 0.001 in with 0.100 in of travel per revolution. During a check, the revolution counter shows two full turns and the pointer then stops 37 divisions past zero. How far did the plunger travel?
Two revolutions are 0.200 in and 37 divisions add 0.037 in, for 0.237 in. Getting 0.039 in counts each revolution as a single division instead of 0.100 in.
std
III.A.1
Measured with tools of the same resolution, why does an outside micrometer usually show less error on a shaft diameter than a vernier caliper?
Its larger measuring faces average out the form errors present on the shaft
Its thimble applies a higher contact force that seats the shaft more firmly
Its scale is read on two axes, which cancels the parallax in each reading
Its spindle lies in line with the measured length (Abbe principle)

A micrometer's measuring axis lies on the line of the scale, so small tilts cause little error; a caliper's jaws are offset from its beam, so any jaw play is magnified (Abbe error). Higher contact force does not improve accuracy and can deflect the part or the frame.
std
III.A.1
An inspector mounts a plunger dial indicator at about 20 degrees off perpendicular to a flat surface to check its height variation. What is the effect?
The readings will show more travel than the surface actually moved
The readings will show less travel than the surface actually moved
The readings are unaffected because the plunger is spring loaded
The readings will only be affected when the surface moves downward

With the plunger tilted, it travels farther along its own axis than the surface moves along its normal (cosine error), so readings are too large; the plunger should be set perpendicular. Spring loading keeps contact but does nothing to remove the angle error.
std
III.A.1
Two inspectors read the same steel rule against the same edge. One looks straight down; the other reads from an angle and gets a value about half a division different. What explains the difference?
Thermal growth of the rule during the second reading
Parallax from viewing the graduations at an angle
Wear on the end of the rule that shifts its zero point
Variation in the flatness of the part being measured

Viewing a scale from an angle makes the edge appear against the wrong graduation, so the line of sight must be perpendicular to the scale. End wear would shift both readings equally, not just the one taken at an angle.
std
III.A.1
A shop replaces its dial calipers with digital calipers that display 0.01 mm. A supervisor says the new calipers are therefore more accurate. What is the best response?
That is correct, because a digital readout removes every source of operator error
That is correct, because digital calipers do not need to be calibrated as often
Display resolution is only the smallest step shown; accuracy has to be shown by calibration
Digital readouts are always less accurate than dial readouts at the same resolution

Resolution is the smallest increment the display can show; accuracy is how close the reading is to the true value and depends on the instrument's condition and calibration. Digital readouts remove reading errors such as misread dials but not jaw wear, alignment or measuring force errors.
std
III.A.2
A hole is specified at 10.00–10.05 mm. An inspector checks it with a go/no-go plug gauge, and both the GO and the NO-GO members enter the hole. What should she conclude?
The hole is undersize and should be rejected
The hole is acceptable because the GO member entered
The hole needs a second check with the NO-GO reversed
The hole is oversize and should be rejected

The GO member checks the smallest allowed hole and should enter; the NO-GO member checks the largest and should not. If NO-GO enters, the hole is larger than 10.05 mm. An undersize hole would stop the GO member, which did not happen here.
std
III.A.2
Using a set of pin gauges in 0.001 in steps, a technician finds that the 0.250 in pin enters a hole with a light fit and the 0.251 in pin will not enter. What can he conclude about the hole?
Its smallest diameter lies between about 0.250 and 0.251 in
Its average diameter is exactly 0.2505 in, midway between pins
Its largest diameter is about 0.251 in along its whole depth
Its diameter cannot be estimated without a bore micrometer

A pin that enters fixes the hole's smallest effective diameter at no less than that pin, and the next pin up sets the upper bound, within the pins' own tolerance. A pin cannot reveal taper or out-of-round, so claiming an exact average or a uniform largest size goes beyond the data.
std
III.A.2
An external thread on a bolt will not turn into its GO thread ring gauge. What does this most likely indicate?
The thread is below its minimum pitch diameter and may strip in use
The thread is beyond its maximum material size and may not assemble
The thread is acceptable because the GO gauge is meant to stop on it
The thread pitch is correct but its major diameter is too small

A GO ring gauge represents the largest functional size allowed, so it should screw on freely; if it will not, the thread is too large or its form is off. Undersize pitch diameter is what the NOT GO gauge checks, and that condition would let the GO gauge turn on easily.
std
III.A.2
A plant needs to verify the internal threads of tapped holes in a housing. Which gauge is suited to this check?
A thread ring gauge with GO and NOT GO members
A set of plain pin gauges sized to the minor diameter
A thread plug gauge with GO and NOT GO members
A screw pitch gauge held against the threaded hole

Internal threads are checked with thread plug gauges; the GO member verifies assembly and the NOT GO member verifies the pitch diameter is not too large. Ring gauges are for external threads, and a pitch gauge only identifies the pitch without judging size.
std
III.A.2

A manufacturer builds a dedicated gauge for a bracket: the part passes if it drops onto a set of fixed pins that represent the mating hole pattern. What is the main trade-off of this kind of custom gauge?
It gives full variable data on each hole but takes longer than a CMM
It removes the need for calibration because it has no moving parts
It measures each hole's position more accurately than a CMM can
It gives a quick pass/fail on fit but no variable data to trend

A functional attribute gauge simulates the mating part, so it is quick and simple at the point of use, but it only says pass or fail. It still wears and must be calibrated against its own drawing like any other M&TE.
std
III.A.2
A machine shop builds a special fixture gauge in-house for one part number. How should the gauge be treated before it is used to accept product?
Give it an ID and verify it against its design drawing, then add it to the recall system
Use it as built, since a gauge made in-house to the part drawing is correct by design
Check it once against a good part and then use it without any further calibration
Treat it as a reference-only tool, because custom gauges cannot be traced to standards

A custom gauge is M&TE: it needs unique identification, verification of its critical features against its drawing using traceable equipment, and periodic recalibration. A good part only shows the gauge accepted one part, not that its features are within the gauge tolerance.
std
III.A.2

A technician must build a 1.3725 in gauge block stack from an inch set with series in 0.0001 in, 0.001 in, 0.050 in and 1 in steps. Following the usual method of removing the rightmost digit first, which block does she select first?

Start with the block that clears the last digit: 1.3725 − 0.1005 = 1.2720, then 0.122, 0.150 and 1.000 complete the stack with four blocks. Taking the largest block first does not help, because the fine digits are what limit the choices and must be cleared first.
std
III.A.2
At the end of a shift, an inspector finishes using a wrung stack of steel gauge blocks. What should he do?
Leave the stack wrung together in the case so it is ready for the next shift
Wipe the stack with a dry shop rag and store it on the surface plate overnight
Separate the blocks, clean them, and coat them with a rust preventive before storing
Wash the blocks in water-based coolant to remove oils, then store them uncovered

Blocks left wrung can bond and corrode at the faces, so they are separated, cleaned and protected promptly. A shop rag carries grit that scratches the lapped faces, and water-based coolant promotes rust.
std
III.A.3
Which inspection task is best suited to an optical comparator?
Measuring the depth of a blind bore inside a casting
Measuring the hardness of a heat-treated shaft
Checking the internal diameter of a long tube
Checking the profile of a small thread form

A comparator projects a magnified silhouette of the part's outline onto a screen, which suits small two-dimensional profiles such as thread forms, radii and angles. Internal features that cannot be seen in silhouette, like a blind bore depth, need other tools.
std
III.A.3
An optical comparator is set at 20X. A radius on a part has a tolerance of ±0.05 mm. On the overlay chart, what total width should the tolerance band have?
2.0 mm
1.0 mm
The total tolerance on the part is 0.10 mm, and at 20X it becomes 0.10 × 20 = 2.0 mm on the chart. Using 1.0 mm magnifies only one side of the bilateral tolerance.
std
III.A.3
Before using a 50X overlay chart on an optical comparator, what should the operator confirm first?
That the screen's protractor ring has been set to read zero degrees
That the installed lens is 50X and its magnification has been verified
That the chart was printed on paper rather than on a clear film
That the part's surface finish meets the drawing specification

Chart dimensions are only valid if the actual magnification matches the chart's, so the lens must match and be verified, for example against a glass scale. The protractor setting matters for angles but does not make a 50X chart read correctly through a different lens.
std
III.A.3
An inspector needs to measure the width of a fine scratch on a polished flat surface without touching it. Which tool fits best?
An outside micrometer with flat carbide measuring faces
A set of pin gauges laid across the width of the scratch
A measuring microscope with a calibrated reticle or stage
A vernier height gauge sweeping across the polished face

A measuring (toolmaker's) microscope magnifies surface features and measures them with a calibrated reticle or stage, without contact. Contact tools such as a micrometer or height gauge cannot resolve or reach a feature this fine and could damage the surface.
std
III.A.3
A lab uses a microscope with an eyepiece reticle to measure small features. How should the reticle's scale be verified?
Accept the scale value printed by the maker for every objective
Measure a part with a caliper and adjust the reticle reading to match
Check it once at the lowest objective and apply that to all others
Compare it to a traceable stage micrometer at each objective used

The reticle's value per division changes with each objective, so it is verified at each magnification against a traceable stage micrometer. A caliper is far coarser than the microscope, so using it as the reference would introduce error.
std
III.A.4
Before a CMM program measures the features of a machined part, what must first be established?
A part coordinate system aligned to the drawing datums
A machine zero set at the near corner of the granite table
A nominal value typed in for every feature in the program
A rough manual check of each feature with hand tools

Feature locations are reported relative to the datum reference frame, so the CMM must first build a part coordinate system from the datum features. The machine's own zero is fixed by its scales and does not relate the measurements to the part.
std
III.A.4
A CMM operator changes to a longer stylus on the touch probe. What should she do before measuring parts?
Measure a production part and compare the result with the last run
Qualify the stylus on the reference sphere before use
Increase the probing speed so the longer stylus reaches features faster
Proceed directly, since the program already knows the stylus length

Qualification against the calibrated reference sphere tells the software the effective tip diameter and position, which change with every stylus. Comparing to a previous part does not separate stylus error from part variation.
std
III.A.4
A thin rubber gasket must be checked for its flat outline and hole positions. It deflects when touched with even light force. Which CMM sensor is best suited?
A touch-trigger probe
A scanning contact probe
A vision system
A mechanical dial indicator

A vision sensor measures edges optically without contact, which suits thin, flexible, mostly two-dimensional parts. A touch-trigger probe needs contact force to register a point, which would deflect the gasket.
std
III.A.4
Engineers need a dense set of points over the freeform surface of a cast housing to compare with its CAD model. Compared with a touch probe, what does a laser line scanner offer?
Higher accuracy on each point and no sensitivity to the color or finish of the scanned surface
Better access to deep internal bores, because the beam can reach places a stylus cannot
The same data as a touch probe, gathered more slowly but with less need for part fixturing
Many more points captured quickly, with lower accuracy per point and sensitivity to shiny surfaces

Laser scanners capture large point clouds fast, which suits freeform surfaces and CAD comparison, but individual points are usually less accurate than touch probing and reflective or dark surfaces can affect results. A beam needs line of sight, so deep internal bores are harder for a laser, not easier.
std
III.A.5
A dimension is specified as 25.00 ± 0.02 mm. Using the 10:1 rule for resolution, which digital display resolution is the coarsest acceptable choice?

The total tolerance is 0.04 mm, and one tenth of that is 0.004 mm, so the display must resolve at least that finely; 0.001 mm is the only option that qualifies. A 0.005 mm display is just coarser than 0.004 mm, and 0.01 mm results from using one side of the tolerance instead of the total.
std
III.A.5
An electronic height gauge with a digital display is moved to a new surface plate. What should the operator do before measuring with it?
Use it as is, since the display holds its last zero
Zero or preset it on the plate or a known gauge block
Turn up the display resolution to its finest setting
Recalibrate it at the lab before it can be used again

A digital display reads relative to the reference it was last set to, so it is zeroed on the plate or preset on a known gauge block at the new setup. Changing the resolution only alters the number of digits shown, not the reference.
std
III.A.5
A cell connects its electronic gauges' data output directly to the SPC software instead of having operators write readings down. What is the main quality benefit?
It improves the accuracy of each gauge by averaging repeated readings
It extends the calibration interval of each gauge that is connected
It removes transcription errors and time-stamps each reading
It removes the need to train operators on how to use the gauges
Direct data output eliminates miscopied or invented numbers and timestamps readings as they occur. It does nothing to the gauge's own accuracy or calibration needs.
std
III.A.6
How should a technician handle precision test weights when checking an analytical balance?
With bare hands, after washing and drying them well
With a clean shop rag wrapped around each weight
With any convenient method, since weights are durable
With tweezers or clean gloves, never with bare hands
Skin oils and moisture add mass and promote corrosion, so precision weights are handled with tweezers or lint-free gloves. Even clean hands leave residue, and a shop rag can leave fibers and grit.
std
III.A.6
An electronic balance arrives calibrated from the supplier and is installed on a lab bench. What should be done before it is used?
Level it and verify or calibrate it in place with test weights
Use it as delivered, since the calibration certificate is current
Tare it once with an empty container and then begin weighing
Send it to an outside lab to repeat the supplier's calibration

Electronic balances sense force, so readings depend on local gravity, leveling and the installation, and they are verified or calibrated where they are used. Taring only zeroes the display; it does not check the balance against known masses.
std
III.A.6
During a routine check, a balance reads 200.6 g with a 200.000 g test weight. Its tolerance at this load is ±0.5 g. What is the right conclusion?
It is in tolerance because 0.6 g is close to the 0.5 g limit
It is out of tolerance by 0.1 g and must be removed from use
It is in tolerance because the error is only 0.3 percent
It is out of tolerance by 0.6 g and must be scrapped

The error is +0.6 g against a ±0.5 g limit, so it exceeds tolerance by 0.1 g; the balance is taken out of service and its recent use evaluated. Calling it in tolerance because it is close ignores the stated limit.
std
III.A.6
A shipping department weighs pallets on a platform scale, and pallets are often set down off-center. Which check best shows whether this affects the readings?
Place a test weight at the center only and compare it to its value
Weigh one pallet twice in the same position and compare the results
Place the same test weight at each corner and the center and compare
Zero the scale at the start of each shift with the platform empty

A corner (eccentricity) test shows whether the reading changes with load position, which is the concern for off-center pallets. Repeating a weighing in the same spot only tests repeatability, not position sensitivity.
std
III.A.7
An inspector notices that nearly all work on a granite surface plate is done in the same area near its center. What is the risk?
The granite will absorb shop heat in that area and bow permanently
The plate will become magnetized where steel parts are placed often
The plate's grade will improve there as the surface becomes polished
Local wear will lower that area and the plate's flatness will degrade

Repeated use in one spot wears it low, so work is spread over the whole plate and flatness is rechecked at intervals. Granite does not become magnetized, which is one of its advantages over cast iron.
std
III.A.7
How is the flatness of a granite surface plate typically verified in service?
By a survey with a repeat-reading gauge and electronic levels
By checking a gauge block stack at one spot near the center of the plate surface
By placing a straightedge along one edge and looking for light under its length
By measuring its thickness at each corner with a large outside micrometer

Flatness is surveyed over the whole working surface, with a repeat-reading gauge for local variation and electronic levels or an autocollimator for overall flatness. A single spot or one edge cannot reveal the plate's overall flatness.
std
III.A.7
A 5 in sine bar is used on a surface plate to set an angle of 30°. What height of gauge block stack is needed under the raised roll?
Stack height equals sine bar length × sin θ = 5 × 0.5 = 2.5000 in. A result of 4.3301 in uses cosine instead of sine.
std
III.A.7
On a surface plate, an indicator on a height stand is zeroed on a 1.2500 in gauge block stack and then swept over a part step, where it reads +0.0008 in. What is the step height?

In comparison measurement the indicator gives the difference from the master, so 1.2500 + 0.0008 = 1.2508 in. Subtracting the reading gives 1.2492 in, which reverses the sign of a higher-than-master reading.
std
III.A.8
A stylus profilometer records these deviations from the mean line at equal spacing: +2, −1, +3, −2, +1, −3 µm. What is Ra?
0 µm
3.0 µm
6.0 µm
2.0 µm
Ra is the arithmetic mean of the absolute deviations: (2 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 3) / 6 = 2.0 µm. Averaging the signed values gives 0, because deviations about the mean line cancel by definition.
std
III.A.8
A turned shaft has a clear lay of circumferential tool marks. In which direction should the profilometer trace?
Across the lay, along the shaft's axis
Along the lay, around the circumference
At about 45° to the lay, as a compromise
In any direction, since Ra does not change
Tracing perpendicular to the lay crosses the tool marks and captures the surface's roughness, which is the usual convention. Tracing along the marks would follow a groove and understate roughness.
std
III.A.8
What does the cutoff length setting on a profilometer control?
How deep the diamond stylus tip is allowed to press into the surface profile
Which long wavelengths are filtered out as waviness
How far the stylus travels before the instrument stops and prints a result
Which peaks are ignored as dirt because they rise above the trace average

The cutoff is a filter wavelength: features longer than it are treated as waviness and removed from roughness parameters such as Ra. Total traverse length is a separate setting, usually several cutoff lengths long.
std
III.A.9
How should a click-type torque wrench be stored at the end of a shift?
Set to the highest value on its scale
Set to the value used most in the shift
Set to the lowest value on its scale
Set to the midpoint of its working range

Storing a click wrench at its lowest setting relieves the internal spring so it does not take a set and drift. Storing it at a high setting keeps the spring compressed and causes the drift the practice is meant to prevent.
std
III.A.9
A torque wrench is checked at a setting of 100 N·m on a torque analyzer. The tolerance is ±4% of the setting, and the analyzer reads 105.5 N·m. What is the result?
In tolerance, since the upper limit is 105.5 N·m
In tolerance, since the error is under 6 percent
Out of tolerance, since the lower limit is 105.0 N·m
Out of tolerance, since the upper limit is 104.0 N·m
Four percent of 100 N·m is 4 N·m, so the limits are 96.0–104.0 N·m, and 105.5 N·m is above them. Calling it in tolerance by using a looser percentage than the stated 4% ignores the requirement.
std
III.A.9
A technician applies a force of 30 lbf, perpendicular to the handle, at a point 1.5 ft from the center of the fastener. What torque is applied?
45 lbf·ft
20 lbf·ft
31.5 lbf·ft
540 lbf·ft
Torque is force times the perpendicular distance: 30 × 1.5 = 45 lbf·ft. Dividing gives 20 lbf·ft, and 540 comes from converting feet to inches (18 in) but labeling the result in lbf·ft.
std
III.A.9
A cell uses a tensometer to pull-test crimped wire terminals. How should the tensometer's force readings be verified?
Pull-test a terminal that passed last week and confirm a similar reading
Apply known, traceable loads across its range and compare
Compare its readings with those from a second tensometer of the same model
Check that its display reads zero with no load before each pull test

A tensometer is verified by applying known, traceable forces across its range, for example dead weights, a calibrated load cell or a proving ring. A second uncalibrated tester of the same model gives agreement, not accuracy.
std
III.A.9
A fastener must be tightened to 12 N·m. The only wrench at the station has a range of 20–200 N·m. What should the technician do?
Use the wrench at its lowest setting of 20 N·m
Set it to 12 N·m by estimating below the scale
Get a wrench whose working range covers 12 N·m
Use it with a short extension to reduce the torque

A torque wrench is only calibrated and reliable within its stated range, and 12 N·m is below it. Tightening to 20 N·m overtorques the joint, and an extension changes the effective length in a way that increases applied torque rather than reducing it.
std
III.B.1
An inspector finds a micrometer in the gauge crib with no ID number and no calibration label. What should she do?
Use it for now, then report it to the calibration lab once the shift has been completed
Check it against a gauge block and use it if the reading falls within the usual tolerance
Apply a new calibration label with today's date so others know it has been reviewed
Segregate it and keep it out of use until it is identified and its calibration is verified

Equipment whose calibration status cannot be determined must not be used for acceptance until it is identified and its status established. A single spot check is not a calibration, and labeling it without calibrating it would falsify its status.
std
III.B.1
A dial indicator is used only to check whether a fixture is roughly level during setup and never for product acceptance. How should it be controlled?
Label it reference only or calibration not required and keep it out of acceptance use
Leave it unlabeled, since equipment not used for acceptance needs no identification
Calibrate it on the same interval as the acceptance gauges to keep the system simple
Remove it from the plant, since every indicator on site must be fully calibrated

Equipment that does not need calibration should be clearly identified so nobody mistakes it for a calibrated device. Leaving it unlabeled invites someone to use it for acceptance without knowing its status.
std
III.B.1
An audit finds a pressure gauge in use on a test stand three weeks past its calibration due date. Which control would best prevent this?
A rule that operators check each gauge's label for its due date once a year
A recall system that flags due items and pulls overdue ones
A larger calibration lab staff so each gauge is calibrated more often
A policy that lets overdue gauges stay in use if they show no problems

A recall system schedules calibration ahead of the due date and removes overdue equipment from use, so status does not depend on chance. Checking labels once a year cannot catch items that fall due in between.
std
III.B.1
A calibration lab has calibrated a pressure gauge on a test stand. What should be done to protect the calibration from tampering?
Lock the gauge in the crib between each use
Record the operator who uses it on each shift
Seal the adjustment points so any change shows
Label it with the date of its next due calibration

Tamper-evident seals on adjustments let users see whether settings were changed after calibration, which would invalidate it. A due-date label shows status but does nothing to stop or reveal an adjustment.
std
III.B.1
A supplier sends a calibration certificate for a set of gauge blocks. Which information best shows that the calibration is traceable?
A statement that the lab holds ISO 9001 certification for its quality management system
The serial number of the gauge set and a stamp from the lab's quality manager on the form
A pass result for each block with the date of calibration and the next due date shown
The reference standards used, their traceability to national standards, and the uncertainty

Traceability is an unbroken chain of comparisons to national or international standards, each with a stated uncertainty, so the certificate must identify the standards used and the uncertainty. ISO 9001 certification covers a quality system, not the technical competence or traceability of the measurements.
std
III.B.1
Micrometers used near a grinding machine keep showing rust and sticky spindles at calibration. What is the best maintenance response?
Clean, lightly oil and case them, away from the coolant
Shorten their calibration interval so the rust is caught earlier at each check
Leave them on the machine table so they stay at the same temperature as parts
Spray them with water-based coolant at the end of each shift to wash off the grit
Routine cleaning, light oiling and protected storage prevent the corrosion and grit that cause sticky spindles. A shorter interval only finds the damage sooner; it does not stop it.
std
III.B.2
A customer ships a special gauge to be used for final acceptance of its parts. What should be done when it arrives?
Put it into use at once, since the customer is responsible for its accuracy and condition
Verify its ID, condition and calibration status, record it and add it to the recall system
Recalibrate and adjust it to the plant's own standards before releasing it for production
Store it unopened until the customer's quality engineer visits to inspect it in person

Customer-supplied equipment is verified on receipt and then controlled like the plant's own: identified, recorded and tracked for calibration. Adjusting customer property without agreement could invalidate the customer's own calibration and should not be done on the plant's initiative.
std
III.B.2
A customer-owned fixture gauge is dropped and a locating pin is bent. What is the right response?
Straighten the pin and check the gauge against a production part
Replace the pin with one from the plant's stock and keep using it
Segregate it, record the damage and report it to the customer
Continue using it until the customer asks for it to be returned

Damage to customer property must be reported to the customer, and the gauge kept out of use until repair or replacement is agreed and it is verified. Repairing it unilaterally and checking it against a part does not establish that it meets its design.
std
III.B.2
A customer-supplied gauge will reach its calibration due date halfway through a long contract. Who calibrates it?
The plant's own lab, without telling the customer, since the gauge is on the plant's premises
No one until the contract ends, because the customer issued the gauge already calibrated
The customer, who must collect it, since the plant may not handle calibration of the property
Whoever was agreed with the customer, with the plant's recall system still flagging the due date

Responsibility for calibrating customer-owned equipment should be set by agreement, and the plant still tracks the due date so the gauge is not used past it. Letting it run past due until the contract ends would mean accepting product with equipment of unknown status.
std
III.C.1
A thread plug gauge is to be recalibrated every 4,000 uses. It is used about 250 times a week. How often should it be scheduled for calibration?
Every 16 weeks
Every 4 weeks
Every 160 weeks
Every 1.6 weeks
4,000 uses ÷ 250 uses per week = 16 weeks. The 1.6 and 160 week answers come from slipping the decimal place.
std
III.C.1
Two identical micrometers are used in a plant. One checks a safety-critical brake component; the other checks a cosmetic trim feature. How should their calibration intervals compare?
Both should have the same interval because the micrometers are identical
The brake micrometer should have the shorter, more conservative interval
The trim micrometer should have the shorter interval because it is used more
The brake micrometer should have the longer interval to limit its handling

Risk-based intervals weigh the consequence of an undetected out-of-tolerance condition, which is far greater for a safety-critical part. Identical models can still warrant different intervals when their use and risk differ.
std
III.C.1

A height gauge has been found in tolerance, with little drift, at each of its last eight 6-month calibrations. The procedure allows a 25% extension after such a record. What new interval should be set?
6.25 months
8 months
7.5 months
4.5 months

A 25% extension of 6 months is 1.5 months, giving 7.5 months; consistent in-tolerance history supports a longer interval. Using 4.5 months applies the change as a reduction, which is what an out-of-tolerance history would call for.
std
III.C.1
A new type of digital force gauge arrives with no calibration history at the plant. How should its first calibration interval be set?
Start with the longest interval the system allows and shorten it if a failure appears
Use the same interval as the oldest gauge in the plant so the schedule stays uniform
Wait until it fails a check in use, then calibrate it on that period going forward
Start from the maker's recommendation, adjusted for use and risk, then refine with history

With no history, the initial interval comes from the manufacturer's recommendation and the expected usage, environment and criticality, then is adjusted as calibration data builds up. Starting at the longest interval maximizes the risk of using an out-of-tolerance gauge before any data exist.
std
III.C.1
