A gauge was calibrated on March 15 and has a 6-month interval. On the plant's schedule, by what date must it be recalibrated or removed from use?
September 15
September 1
June 15
March 15 of next year
March 15 plus 6 months is September 15, after which the gauge is overdue. June 15 is a 3-month interval and March 15 of next year a 12-month one.
std
III.C.2
A calibration certificate shows a gauge was out of tolerance as found and in tolerance as left after adjustment. Which data matter for judging product measured since the last calibration?
The as-left data
The as-found data
The adjustment made
The next due date
As-found readings describe the gauge's condition while it was being used on product, so they drive the impact assessment. As-left readings only show its condition from now on.
std
III.C.2
A shaft is specified at 12.00 ± 0.05 mm. At calibration, the micrometer used to accept shafts is found to read 0.03 mm high. Which accepted shafts are suspect?
Those recorded from 12.02 mm up to the 12.05 mm upper limit
Those recorded within 0.03 mm of the 12.00 mm nominal size
Those recorded from 11.95 mm up to just under 11.98 mm
None, since a 0.03 mm error is smaller than the ±0.05 mm tolerance

Reading high means true size = reading − 0.03, so shafts recorded below 11.98 mm may truly be under the 11.95 mm lower limit. Shafts near the upper limit are actually smaller than recorded, so they are safe; some shafts rejected as oversize may in fact have been good.
std
III.C.2
A gauge used to accept product shipped to a customer is found out of tolerance at calibration, and the evaluation shows some shipped product may be nonconforming. What should the plant do?
Recalibrate the gauge and continue, since the product has already shipped
Scrap all product in the plant made since the last good calibration date
Shorten the gauge's calibration interval and record no further action
Trace the affected lots and notify the customer about the suspect product

When previous results may be invalid, the plant traces affected product and acts on it, including telling the customer about suspect shipments. Recalibrating fixes the gauge going forward but does nothing about product already accepted with it.
std
III.C.2
A gauge missed two scheduled calibrations. When finally calibrated, it is found in tolerance. What is the best conclusion?
Product it measured is probably fine, but the lapse is a system failure to correct
No action is needed, since the in-tolerance result shows the schedule was too short
All product measured with the gauge since the last calibration must be scrapped
The gauge should be retired, since an overdue gauge can no longer be trusted

An in-tolerance as-found result suggests past measurements were valid, but the missed calibrations are still a breakdown in control that must be documented and corrected. One good result is not enough evidence to lengthen the interval on its own.
std
III.C.2
A pressure gauge was found out of tolerance at three of its last four calibrations. What should be done?
Keep the interval and adjust it more carefully each time
Shorten its interval and look into why it keeps drifting
Lengthen its interval to reduce handling during transport
Keep the interval but stop recording the as-found results

Repeated out-of-tolerance findings show the interval is too long for this gauge's stability, so it is shortened and the cause or suitability of the gauge investigated. Adjusting more carefully at calibration does not stop drift between calibrations.
std
III.C.2
A height gauge's as-found error has grown about +0.001 mm at each 6-month calibration and was +0.003 mm at the last one. Its tolerance is ±0.004 mm. What does the trend suggest?
It is well within tolerance, so the interval can be lengthened at the next calibration
It has stopped drifting, because +0.003 mm is below the tolerance of ±0.004 mm
It will likely be at or beyond its limit by the next due date, so shorten the interval
It should be scrapped now, because any measurable drift shows the gauge has failed

At +0.001 mm per interval, the next as-found would be about +0.004 mm, right at the limit, with no margin, so the interval should be shortened or the gauge adjusted sooner. Being in tolerance today does not mean it will be at the next due date.
std
III.C.2
A technician finds a gauge out of tolerance, adjusts it, and records only "adjusted, OK" with the date. What is the main gap in the record?
The name of the person who last used the gauge on product
The cost of the labor spent adjusting the gauge at the lab
The serial number of the bench where the gauge was adjusted
The as-found readings needed to judge impact on product

Without the as-found data, nobody can tell how far out the gauge was or which product decisions might be affected. A full record also includes as-left data, standards used, procedure, date, technician and next due date.
std
III.C.3
A 100 mm steel gauge block (expansion coefficient 11.5 × 10⁻⁶ per °C) is used at 25 °C instead of the 20 °C reference temperature. About how much longer is it than its stated length?
Growth = 100 mm × 11.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 5 °C ≈ 0.00575 mm, or about 0.006 mm. The 0.029 mm answer uses the full 25 °C instead of the 5 °C difference from reference.
std
III.C.3
A set of gauges is carried in from a cold loading dock and calibrated right away in the lab. What is the main risk?
Error from the lab standards being too warm to read well
Error from the gauges not having reached lab temperature
Error from condensation improving contact on the faces
Error from the operator's hands being colder than usual

Gauges must soak to the lab's controlled temperature before calibration, or thermal size differences between gauge and standard show up as calibration error. Condensation does not improve anything; it adds a film and promotes corrosion.
std
III.C.3
A lab sets all its bore gauges from one master ring gauge. The ring has worn 0.004 mm oversize over the years without anyone noticing. What effect does this have?
Each bore gauge gets a different random error
The bore gauges are unaffected because they are adjustable
Every bore gauge set from it carries the same bias
Only the bore gauges used most often pick up the error

An error in a standard is passed as a systematic bias to everything calibrated or set from it, which is why standards themselves are calibrated on a schedule. The error is not random; it shifts all the gauges the same way.
std
III.C.3
Two technicians calibrate the same micrometer against the same gauge blocks. One uses the ratchet stop; the other tightens the thimble by feel. Their results differ. What is the most likely cause?
A defective gauge block in the set that both of them used
A loose ratchet stop on the micrometer's thimble assembly
A difference in the lab temperature between the two checks
Inconsistent measuring force from different technique

Turning the thimble by feel applies varying force, while the ratchet gives consistent force; the calibration procedure should specify the method. A defective block would affect both technicians' results the same way.
std
III.C.3
Because of a calibration error, a gauge reads 0.01 mm low. Operators adjust a lathe to keep the gauge readings centered on nominal. What happens to the parts?
The parts actually run about 0.01 mm larger than intended
The parts actually run about 0.01 mm smaller than intended
The parts are unaffected, since the operators center the process
The parts become more variable but stay centered on nominal

If the gauge reads 0.01 mm low, a reading at nominal means the true size is 0.01 mm above nominal, so the process is centered off target. Centering on a biased gauge locks the bias into the product instead of removing it.
std
III.C.3
A gauge with an undetected calibration bias is used for final acceptance. Which pair of outcomes can result?
Higher scrap costs only, with no risk to customers
Accepting some bad parts and rejecting some good ones
More variation in the process but no effect on decisions
Accepting some bad parts but never rejecting good ones

A biased gauge shifts every decision, so near one limit bad parts look good (consumer's risk) and near the other good parts look bad (producer's risk). Which limit sees which depends on the direction of the bias, but both errors occur.
std
III.C.4
Which statement best describes a primary standard?
It is the most accurate gauge kept in a company lab and calibrated by an outside lab
It is the gauge used most often on the shop floor to accept production parts
It is a top-level standard, usually held by a national institute, that realizes the unit
It is a portable device used to carry a value from one lab to another site

A primary standard sits at the top of the chain and realizes the SI unit directly, typically at a national metrology institute. A company's best in-house standard calibrated by an outside lab is a reference standard, not a primary one.
std
III.C.4
A company's calibration lab keeps one high-grade gauge block set that is used only to calibrate its working gauge blocks and is itself sent to an accredited lab. What level is this set?
A primary standard
A working standard
A shop gauge
A reference standard
A reference standard is the highest-accuracy standard at a location, from which that location's measurements are derived. It is not primary, because it gets its value from a higher-level lab.
std
III.C.4
A proving ring is calibrated at an accredited lab and then taken to a plant to compare against and calibrate its tensile testers. In this role, the proving ring serves as:
A transfer standard
A primary standard
A shop-floor gauge
An attribute gauge

A transfer standard carries a known value from one standard or location to another, as the proving ring does between the lab and the plant's testers. It is not primary, since it was itself calibrated against higher standards.
std
III.C.4
A shop gauge has a tolerance of ±0.020 mm. The lab requires a 4:1 accuracy ratio between the gauge and the standard used to calibrate it. What is the largest acceptable uncertainty for the standard?
Dividing the gauge tolerance by 4 gives ±0.020 / 4 = ±0.005 mm. Multiplying instead gives ±0.080 mm, which would make the standard far worse than the gauge.
std
III.C.4
Which order runs from the highest level of standard to the lowest?
Reference, primary, working, shop gauge
Primary, working, reference, shop gauge
Primary, reference, working, shop gauge
Working, reference, primary, shop gauge

Values flow from national primary standards to a lab's reference standards, then to working standards used to calibrate everyday shop gauges. Placing working above reference reverses the lab's internal chain.
std
III.C.4
Why does measurement uncertainty generally increase at each lower level of the standards hierarchy?
Lower-level standards are usually made from less stable types of material
Lower levels are calibrated less often than the higher levels in the chain
Each level is allowed to round its values to fewer significant digits
Each calibration step adds its own uncertainty to that of the level above

Each comparison in the chain contributes uncertainty from the method, environment and instrument, which combines with the uncertainty already carried from above. Materials and intervals vary, but the accumulation through each step is what drives the increase.
std
IV.A.1
A metric drawing's title block gives general tolerances of X.X ±0.1 and X.XX ±0.02. A shaft length is dimensioned 25.40 with no tolerance stated. What range is acceptable?

The dimension has two decimal places, so the X.XX block tolerance of ±0.02 applies, giving 25.38 to 25.42. Applying ±0.1 uses the one-place tolerance, which does not match how the dimension is written.
std
IV.A.1
An inspector receives parts marked revision D, but the drawing packet at her bench is revision C. What should she do before inspecting?
Inspect to revision C, since it is the drawing she has been issued
Inspect to revision D from the part marking and note the gap on the report
Inspect to both revisions and accept the parts if either one is met
Get the revision called out on the order and confirm it is the one she uses

Parts must be inspected to the revision the order or work instruction specifies, so the first step is to obtain and confirm it. Simply trusting the bench copy or the part marking risks inspecting to the wrong requirements.
std
IV.A.1
In the front view of a bracket, a slot on the back face is drawn with short, evenly spaced dashes. What do these lines show?
The center axis of the slot
The edge of a mating part that is not supplied
Edges hidden from view in that projection
The path of a cutting plane for a section view
Short dashed lines are hidden lines, showing edges behind visible surfaces. Centerlines and phantom lines use long and short dashes, and a cutting-plane line is a heavy line ending in arrows.
std
IV.A.1
A drawing shows the third-angle projection symbol. Where will the right side view of the part be placed?
To the left of the front view
To the right of the front view
Directly above the front view
Directly below the top view of the part

In third-angle projection each view is placed on the side from which it is seen, so the right side view sits to the right of the front view and the top view above it. Placing the right side view on the left is the first-angle convention.
std
IV.A.1
A housing drawing includes a section view. What does the crosshatching on that view tell the inspector?
Which surfaces need a machined surface finish
Surfaces cut by the cutting plane
Which areas are hidden behind other features
Where welds are to be placed on the assembly

Section lining marks the surfaces that the imaginary cutting plane slices through, which shows internal features such as wall thickness. Hidden features are shown with dashed lines, and finish and weld requirements have their own symbols.
std
IV.A.1
A hole callout reads: ⌀8.5 THRU, ⌴ ⌀14 ↧ 6. What should the inspector check?
An 8.5 through hole with a 14 counterbore that is 6 deep
An 8.5 through hole with a 14 countersink at 6 degrees
A 14 through hole with an 8.5 spotface that is 6 deep
An 8.5 hole that is 6 deep with a 14 counterbore on top

⌴ is the counterbore symbol and ↧ is depth, so the callout is an 8.5 through hole counterbored to 14 diameter, 6 deep. A countersink uses the ⌵ symbol, and THRU means the 8.5 hole goes all the way through.
std
IV.A.1
A dimension of 42.0 on a drawing is shown in parentheses. How should the inspector treat it?
As a basic dimension
As a critical dimension that must be measured on every part
As a dimension held to the title block general tolerance
As information only, not as an inspection requirement
A dimension in parentheses is a reference dimension, usually derived from other dimensions, and is not used for acceptance. A basic dimension is shown in a box, not in parentheses.
std
IV.A.1
A hole location on a drawing is given as 30.00 inside a rectangular box, with no ± tolerance beside it. Where does the inspector find the allowed variation?
In the general tolerance block of the title block
In the note that says do not scale the drawing
In the feature control frame that applies to the hole
Nowhere, because boxed values have no tolerance at all

A boxed value is a basic dimension: it defines the theoretically exact location, and the tolerance comes from the related feature control frame, such as a position tolerance. Title block tolerances do not apply to basic dimensions.
std
IV.A.1
A dimension needed to check a part is missing from the drawing, and the drawing is marked "Do not scale." What should the inspector do?
Measure the printed view with a scale and convert the value
Use the value measured on a part that has already been accepted
Ask engineering to supply or clarify the missing requirement
Skip the feature because it has no stated requirement to meet

A missing dimension is a drawing problem only the design authority can resolve, and "Do not scale" forbids taking values off the print. Using a previously accepted part assumes that part was right, which is not a requirement.
std
IV.A.1
A drawing has a flag note symbol, a triangle containing the number 4, pointing to one edge. General note 4 reads "Break edge 0.2 to 0.5." Where does the requirement apply?
To every edge on the part
Only to the edge the flag note points to
To all edges listed in the title block material entry
Only to edges on the views that have the same flag

A flagged note applies only where the flag is placed, while an unflagged general note applies to the whole drawing. Treating the flagged note as general would add a requirement the designer did not intend.
std
IV.A.2
A hole is dimensioned ⌀10.1 ±0.1 with a position tolerance of ⌀0.2 at MMC. The hole measures ⌀10.15. What position tolerance is allowed for this hole?

The MMC of a hole is its smallest size, 10.0, so the bonus is 10.15 − 10.0 = 0.15 and the allowed position tolerance is 0.2 + 0.15 = 0.35. Answering 0.25 measures the bonus from the nominal size instead of from MMC.
std
IV.A.2
A pin is dimensioned ⌀12.0 ±0.1 with a position tolerance of ⌀0.1 at MMC. The pin measures ⌀11.95. What position tolerance is allowed?

For an external feature MMC is the largest size, 12.1, so the bonus is 12.1 − 11.95 = 0.15 and the total is 0.1 + 0.15 = 0.25. Answering 0.15 takes the bonus from the nominal 12.0 rather than from MMC.
std
IV.A.2
A CMM finds a hole center 0.06 mm off true position in X and 0.08 mm off in Y. The position tolerance is ⌀0.15 with no modifier. What is the result?
Actual position ⌀0.10, so the hole is accepted
Actual position ⌀0.14, so the hole is accepted
Actual position ⌀0.28, so the hole is rejected
Actual position ⌀0.20, so the hole is rejected
The radial offset is √(0.06² + 0.08²) = 0.10, and a diametral zone doubles it to ⌀0.20, which exceeds ⌀0.15. Answering ⌀0.10 forgets to double the radial value for a cylindrical tolerance zone.
std
IV.A.2
A hole is toleranced ⌀8.0 to ⌀8.2 with position ⌀0.1 at MMC. A part has a hole of ⌀8.12 and a measured position error of ⌀0.18. What is the correct decision?
Reject, because ⌀0.18 is more than the ⌀0.1 stated
Reject, because the bonus only applies at the MMC size
Accept, because the allowed tolerance at this size is ⌀0.22
Accept, because position does not apply above ⌀8.1

Bonus equals the departure from MMC: 8.12 − 8.0 = 0.12, so the allowed tolerance is 0.1 + 0.12 = 0.22 and ⌀0.18 conforms. Rejecting against ⌀0.1 ignores the MMC modifier, and the stated value is the tolerance at MMC, not the only one allowed.
std
IV.A.2
A position tolerance on a hole has no material condition modifier. The hole is made near its largest allowed size. How much bonus tolerance applies?
The full difference between the actual size and MMC
None, because the tolerance applies regardless of feature size
Half the difference between the actual size and LMC
Whatever the inspector judges the mating part allows
Under Y14.5 a tolerance with no modifier applies regardless of feature size (RFS), so no bonus is earned. Bonus is available only when MMC or LMC is specified.
std
IV.A.2
A designer applies a position tolerance at LMC to a hole close to a part edge. What is the most likely purpose?
To protect minimum wall at the edge
To make sure a mating pin always assembles freely
To let the hole be checked with a fixed functional gauge
To keep the hole round within its size tolerance limits
LMC control limits how far a hole at its largest size can drift, which protects minimum wall or edge distance. Assured assembly and functional gauging are the purposes of an MMC callout.
std
IV.A.2
A feature control frame reads: position ⌀0.2 Ⓜ | B | A | C. How should the part be set up for inspection?
Seat datum B first, then contact A, then C
Seat datum A first, then contact B, then C
Seat datum C first, then contact B, then A
Contact all three datums at the same time

Datums are applied in the order listed in the frame, not in alphabetical order, so B is primary, A secondary and C tertiary. Setting up A first would build a different datum reference frame and could change the result.
std
IV.A.2
When a part's primary datum is a flat surface, how many points of contact does it need with the datum simulator to establish the datum plane?
At least two
Exactly one
At least four, one per corner
At least three

A primary planar datum is established by a minimum of three points of contact, the secondary by two and the tertiary by one. Two points is the minimum for a secondary datum, which only needs to stop rotation once the primary plane is set.
std
IV.A.2
Each cross-section of a shaft passes its circularity check, but the shaft tapers along its length. Which control would also catch the taper?
Circularity at more sections
Flatness
Cylindricity
Angularity

Cylindricity applies one tolerance zone to the whole surface, so it controls circularity, straightness and taper together. Circularity checks each cross-section on its own, so adding more sections still would not catch a gradual taper.
std
IV.A.2
A pin is dimensioned ⌀20.00 ±0.05 with no form callout. Under Rule #1 of ASME Y14.5, what limits its straightness?
It may bend freely as long as each size reading passes
It must fit inside a perfect cylinder of ⌀20.05
It must be straight within 0.05 at any size
It must fit inside a perfect cylinder of ⌀20.00

Rule #1 requires perfect form at MMC, so the pin's surface may not go outside a perfect-form envelope at its largest size, ⌀20.05. Local size checks alone would allow a bent pin that will not assemble.
std
IV.A.2
A drawing shows a flatness tolerance with a datum reference in the feature control frame. What should the inspector do?
Measure flatness relative to the datum as written
Ask engineering to correct the callout
Ignore the datum and check flatness as parallelism
Accept the part on size alone and skip the flatness

Form tolerances such as flatness control a feature on its own and are never related to a datum, so the callout is an error for the design authority to fix. Measuring it as parallelism would apply a different control than the one specified.
std
IV.A.2
A face has a perpendicularity tolerance of 0.05 to datum A. What tolerance zone applies to the face?
Two parallel planes 0.05 apart, perpendicular to datum A
Two parallel planes 0.05 apart, parallel to datum A
A cylinder ⌀0.05 whose axis is perpendicular to datum A
Two planes 0.05 apart located at a basic distance from A

For a surface, perpendicularity is an orientation control with a zone of two parallel planes at 90° to the datum. A cylindrical zone applies to an axis only when ⌀ is shown, and a basic distance from the datum would make it a location control.
std
IV.A.2

A surface has a profile of a surface tolerance of 0.4 to datums A, B and C, equally disposed about the true profile. A CMM reports deviations of +0.15, −0.18 and +0.22 at three points. What is the result?
Accept, because every deviation is within ±0.4
Accept, because the average deviation is within 0.2
Reject, because −0.18 is closer to the lower limit
Reject, because +0.22 is outside the ±0.2 zone
An equally disposed 0.4 profile zone extends 0.2 each side of the true profile, so +0.22 is outside it. Reading the zone as ±0.4 doubles the tolerance.
std
IV.A.2
A shaft has a circular runout tolerance of 0.04 to datum axis A. Indicator readings (FIM) at three sections are 0.03, 0.05 and 0.04. What is the result?
Accept, because the average runout is 0.04
Accept, because two of the three sections pass
Reject, because one section has 0.05 of runout
Reject, because the readings add up to 0.12
Circular runout applies to each circular element on its own, so the 0.05 section fails. Averaging or adding sections is not how circular runout is evaluated.
std
IV.A.2
What is the main difference between checking circular runout and total runout on a shaft?
For total runout the part is checked between centers instead of in a vee block
For circular runout the readings at all sections are added together
For total runout the indicator travels along the whole surface while it rotates
For circular runout no datum axis is needed for the part to rotate on
Total runout sweeps the indicator along the full surface, so it also controls taper and straightness; circular runout checks each cross-section separately. Both runout controls require a datum axis.
std
IV.A.3
A batch of brake caliper bolts is found to have missed heat treatment. How should this defect be classified?
Major, because the bolts will not assemble properly
Critical, because it could cause an unsafe condition
Minor, because the bolts still meet their size limits
Major, because heat treatment is a special process
A defect likely to create a hazardous or unsafe condition is critical, and an under-strength brake bolt can fail in service. Correct dimensions do not offset a loss of strength in a safety part.
std
IV.A.3
A connector is wired with two pins swapped, so the device will not work, but there is no safety risk. How should this be classified?
Major
Critical
Minor
Incidental
A major defect is likely to cause failure or materially reduce usability without creating a hazard. Critical is reserved for defects that are likely to make the product unsafe.
std
IV.A.3

A light scratch is found on the inside of a cabinet panel that the user will not see. The drawing's finish note allows no scratches on any surface, and the scratch does not affect function. How should it be classified?
Major
Critical
Not a defect, since it cannot be seen
Minor

The scratch breaks a stated finish requirement, so it is a defect; because it does not materially reduce usability, it is minor. Being hidden from the user lowers its seriousness but does not remove the departure from the requirement.
std
IV.A.3
An inspected unit has one major defect and three minor defects. How is the unit classified?
As a minor defective
As four separate defectives
As a critical defective
As a major defective
A defective unit is classed by its most serious defect, so this unit is a major defective. The three minor defects are counted as defects but do not make the unit more than one defective.
std
IV.A.3
A plan for a product sets acceptance criteria by defect class. Which arrangement is most appropriate?
The same AQL for every class, so all defects are treated equally
Tightest criteria for minor, since they are the most frequent
Tighter criteria as severity increases
Looser criteria for critical, since they are rarely found

Acceptance criteria get tighter as consequences become more serious, and critical defects often call for zero acceptance or 100% inspection. Using one AQL for all classes would give a safety defect the same allowance as a cosmetic one.
std
IV.A.3
A dimension on a drawing carries the customer's significant characteristic symbol. What does this mean for production and inspection?
It is a reference value and is not checked at final inspection
Its variation affects fit, function or performance and needs special control
It must be verified by the customer before every shipment
It affects user safety and must be inspected on every part

A significant characteristic is one whose variation affects fit, function or performance, so it gets added controls such as SPC in the control plan. Safety and regulatory impact is what a critical characteristic symbol flags.
std
IV.A.3
A weld size on a lifting bracket is marked with the critical characteristic symbol. What does that symbol identify?
A feature whose variation could affect safety or regulatory compliance
A feature whose variation affects fit with a mating part
A feature that was found out of tolerance at first article
A feature that the supplier may measure less often than others

Critical characteristic symbols mark features that affect safety or compliance with regulations, and they drive the strictest controls. Fit with a mating part is the kind of effect a significant characteristic covers.
std
IV.A.3
How do characteristic symbols on a drawing differ from defect classifications such as critical, major and minor?
Symbols flag features in advance; defect classes grade problems found
Symbols are set by inspectors; defect classes are set by designers
Symbols apply only to purchased parts; defect classes apply in-house
Symbols grade problems found; defect classes flag features in advance

Characteristic symbols are assigned during design and planning to show which features need special control, while defect classes rate how serious a nonconformance is once it occurs. The reversed option swaps those two roles.
std
IV.B.1
An inspector reads the length of a block straight off the scale of a digital caliper. What type of measurement is this?
Differential
Derived
Transfer
Direct
A direct measurement gives the value straight from the instrument's scale. Differential compares to a master, derived calculates from other values, and transfer moves a size to another instrument.
std
IV.B.1
An inspector zeros a dial indicator on a gauge block stack of 25.000 mm and then reads +0.012 mm on a part. What type of measurement is this?
Direct
Derived
Differential
Transfer

Measuring the difference from a known master and adding it to the master's value is a differential (comparative) measurement. It is not direct, because the indicator does not read the part's full size.
std
IV.B.1
A technician finds a part's density by weighing it and dividing the mass by its volume calculated from measured dimensions. What type of measurement is this?
Direct
Derived
Differential
Transfer
A derived (indirect) measurement calculates the result from other measured quantities. No single instrument reads density here, so it is not direct.
std
IV.B.1
An inspector sets a telescoping gauge in a bore, locks it, removes it and measures it with an outside micrometer. What type of measurement is this?
Direct
Transfer
Derived
Differential

A telescoping gauge has no scale; it picks up the size and transfers it to an instrument that can read it. The micrometer reading is not direct because the bore itself is never touched by the micrometer.
std
IV.B.1
An angle is set with a sine bar and gauge blocks, and the angle is calculated from the block height and the bar length. What type of measurement is this?
Derived
Transfer
Differential
Direct

The angle is calculated from the measured height and the known bar length using trigonometry, which makes it derived. Gauge blocks are used, but the result is still computed rather than read or compared.
std
IV.B.1
Why is a differential measurement often more accurate than a direct one over the same size range?
The instrument must have a longer scale than a direct one
The result does not depend on the accuracy of the master
The part is measured at more points than in a direct check
The instrument covers only a small span around a precise master
A comparator only reads the small difference from a calibrated master, so its errors act over a short span. The result does depend on the master, so an inaccurate master gives an inaccurate result.
std
IV.B.1
Which task most clearly needs a transfer measurement?
Checking the outside diameter of a pin
Checking the length of a bar with a tape
Checking the width of an internal groove
Checking a part height against a master

An internal groove is hard to reach with a direct-reading instrument, so a small hole or inside gauge picks up the size and a micrometer reads it. An outside diameter can be read directly, and comparing to a master is differential.
std
IV.B.2
A diameter is toleranced 15.00 ±0.02 mm. Using the 10:1 rule, which instrument resolution is the coarsest acceptable?

The total tolerance is 0.04 mm, and one tenth of that is 0.004 mm, so the resolution must be 0.004 mm or finer; of the options only 0.002 mm qualifies. A 0.005 mm instrument is close but still coarser than the 0.004 mm needed.
std
IV.B.2
A digital readout displays to 0.001 mm, but its calibration certificate shows an accuracy of ±0.02 mm. The tolerance is ±0.01 mm. What should the inspector conclude?
It is suitable, because its resolution is ten times the tolerance
It is not suitable, because its accuracy is worse than the tolerance
It is suitable if the reading is repeated and then averaged
It is not suitable, because its display has too many digits

Resolution only says how finely the instrument displays; accuracy says how close the reading is to the true value, and ±0.02 mm swamps a ±0.01 mm tolerance. Averaging repeat readings reduces random error but cannot remove a systematic accuracy error.
std
IV.B.2
A plant wants each gauge's ± accuracy to be at most one quarter of the part's ± tolerance. The part is 40.00 ±0.08 mm. Which gauge meets the rule?
A gauge accurate to ±0.02 mm
A gauge accurate to ±0.04 mm
A gauge accurate to ±0.05 mm
A gauge accurate to ±0.08 mm
One quarter of ±0.08 mm is ±0.02 mm, so only that gauge meets a 4:1 ratio. ±0.04 mm is just 2:1, which leaves much of the tolerance used up by the gauge.
std
IV.B.2
Aluminum castings with a ±0.01 mm bore tolerance come off a hot machining line. The only CMM is in a temperature-controlled lab. What is the best measuring approach?
Measure parts at the machine with a bore gauge right away
Measure parts hot on the CMM and subtract a fixed offset
Measure parts with a caliper on the floor to save time
Let parts soak to lab temperature, then measure them on the CMM

Aluminum grows noticeably with heat, so tight bore checks should be made after the part reaches the controlled reference temperature. A fixed offset assumes every part is at the same temperature, which is rarely true.
std
IV.B.2
An inspector must measure the thickness of a thin, soft plastic film. Which instrument is best?
A ratchet micrometer with standard anvils
A vernier caliper with flat jaws
A dial indicator with a hard pointed tip
A non-contact optical or laser gauge
A soft film deforms under contact force, so a non-contact method gives the true thickness. A ratchet controls force but still compresses the film enough to bias the reading.
std
IV.B.2
An inspector must check the pitch diameter of internal threads on 500 parts per shift for accept or reject. Which gauge fits best?
A thread micrometer
An outside micrometer with thread wires
A go/no-go thread plug gauge
A steel rule and a thread pitch gauge

A go/no-go thread plug quickly checks an internal thread's functional size for accept or reject at high volume. Thread micrometers and three-wire methods are for external threads, and a pitch gauge only identifies pitch.
std
IV.B.2
A gauge will be used next to a press line with heavy vibration, coolant mist and dust. Which factor matters most when choosing it?
Whether its display has the most digits available
Whether it stays reliable in those conditions
Whether it was the cheapest option on the list
Whether it can be used in the lab after the shift
The environment of use must be considered: vibration, coolant and dust can make delicate instruments unreliable. Extra display digits do not help if the reading cannot be trusted in those conditions.
std
IV.B.3
A master ring with a reference value of 25.000 mm is measured five times: 25.010, 25.014, 25.012, 25.011 and 25.013 mm. What is the bias?
Bias is the average reading minus the reference value: 25.012 − 25.000 = +0.012 mm. A sign of −0.012 reverses the subtraction, and 0.004 mm is the range of the readings, not the bias.
std
IV.B.3
A study finds a gauge's bias is +0.002 mm on small masters and +0.020 mm on large masters. What does this show?
A linearity problem across the operating range
A repeatability problem on large parts only
A reproducibility problem between the operators
A stability problem over the period of the study
Linearity is the change in bias across the gauge's range, which is what these results show. Repeatability concerns spread on repeat readings, not a shift in average with size.
std
IV.B.3
A supplier and its customer measure the same 20 parts on their own gauges and compare results. What is this type of study called?
A linearity study
A stability study
A repeatability study
A correlation study

A correlation study checks whether two measurement systems give consistent results on the same parts, which settles disputes between supplier and customer readings. Linearity concerns bias across one gauge's range.
std
IV.B.3
A gauge has a measurement system standard deviation of 0.005 mm. The part is 10.00 ±0.10 mm. Using P/T = 6σ ÷ (USL − LSL), what is the precision-to-tolerance ratio?
P/T = 6 × 0.005 ÷ 0.20 = 0.15, or 15%. Using the half tolerance of 0.10 gives 30%, and leaving out the factor of 6 gives 2.5%.
std
IV.B.3
A gauge study finds repeatability (equipment variation) of 0.03 mm and reproducibility (appraiser variation) of 0.04 mm, as standard deviations. What is the combined gauge R&R?
Variances add, so GRR = √(0.03² + 0.04²) = 0.05 mm. Adding the standard deviations directly gives 0.07 mm, which overstates the combined variation.
std
IV.B.3
A planner sets up a variable gauge R&R study. Which method follows good practice?
Ten identical parts near nominal, one appraiser, repeat trials in fixed order
Ten parts over the process range, three appraisers, repeat trials in random order
Three parts at the limits, three appraisers, one trial each with labels shown
Ten parts over the range, three appraisers, trials in order with the IDs shown

A typical study uses about ten parts spanning the process variation, two or three appraisers and two or three trials, with parts randomized and identities hidden so appraisers cannot recall earlier readings. Using identical parts hides the gauge's ability to tell parts apart.
std
IV.B.3
A gauge R&R study shows that repeatability is much larger than reproducibility. Where should improvement start?
With the gauge itself, such as its condition, fixturing or design
With retraining the appraisers on the measuring method
With replacing the master used to zero the gauge
With collecting more parts that span the process range

Large repeatability means the same appraiser cannot get the same reading twice with the same gauge, which points to the instrument or fixture. Appraiser training targets reproducibility, which is the smaller component here.
std
IV.B.3
A gauge R&R study gives %GRR of 22% of tolerance. Under common AIAG guidelines, how should this be judged?
Acceptable for every use without any review
Unacceptable, and the gauge must be scrapped
Acceptable only if the parts are near nominal
Conditionally acceptable, based on use

Common guidelines treat under 10% as acceptable, 10% to 30% as possibly acceptable depending on importance and cost, and over 30% as unacceptable. 22% therefore needs a judgment, not automatic approval or rejection.
std
IV.B.3
Three inspectors use a go/no-go gauge to judge 50 parts. Why is this studied with an attribute agreement analysis instead of an ANOVA gauge R&R?
The parts are too small to measure
The inspectors have more experience than the operators
The results are pass or fail, not measured values
The gauge does not need regular calibration checks
An attribute gauge only gives a category, so its performance is judged by how often decisions agree with each other and with a reference. ANOVA gauge R&R needs continuous variable readings.
std
IV.B.3

In an attribute study, an appraiser judges 50 reference parts twice. She agrees with herself on 46 parts and matches the reference on both trials for 44 parts. What is her percent agreement with the reference?
Agreement with the reference counts parts where both trials matched the standard: 44 ÷ 50 = 88%. 92% is her within-appraiser agreement, which shows consistency but not correctness.
std
IV.B.3
A gauge R&R study shows the system can distinguish only 2 distinct categories of parts. What does this mean for using it to control the process?
It is ideal for SPC because the results are very stable
It cannot tell parts apart well enough to track process variation
It needs only a new calibration sticker before use
It should be used only by the most skilled appraiser

Guidelines look for five or more distinct categories; two means the system works little better than a pass or fail check and cannot track process variation. A calibration sticker does not change the system's variation.
std
IV.B.4
A value of 12.3489 must be reported to two decimal places. What are the results by truncation and by rounding?
Truncated 12.34; rounded 12.35
Truncated 12.35; rounded 12.34
Truncated 12.34; rounded 12.34
Truncated 12.35; rounded 12.35
Truncation drops the extra digits, giving 12.34; rounding looks at the next digit, 8, and raises the last kept digit to 12.35. Rounding in two stages from the right would not change this result.
std
IV.B.4
A deviation of −4.678 mm must be reported to one decimal place. What are the results by truncation and by rounding?
Truncated −4.7; rounded −4.7
Truncated −4.6; rounded −4.6
Truncated −4.7; rounded −4.6
Truncated −4.6; rounded −4.7

Truncation removes digits, moving the value toward zero, so −4.678 becomes −4.6; rounding works on the magnitude, so 4.678 becomes 4.7 and the result is −4.7. Truncating to −4.7 treats truncation like rounding down to the next lower number.
std
IV.B.4
How many significant figures does 0.004050 have?
Three
Six
Seven
Four
Leading zeros only place the decimal point and are not significant; the digits 4, 0, 5 and the trailing 0 after the decimal are, giving four. Counting every digit after the decimal point gives six.
std
IV.B.4
A length of 12.6 mm is multiplied by a factor of 2.0. How should the product be reported?
25 mm
30 mm

In multiplication the result keeps the fewest significant figures of the inputs; 2.0 has two, so 25.2 is reported as 25. Reporting 25.2 claims three significant figures that the factor does not support.
std
IV.B.4
Three measured lengths, 12.11 mm, 0.3 mm and 1.256 mm, are added. How should the total be reported?
14 mm

In addition the result keeps the fewest decimal places of the inputs; 0.3 has one, so 13.666 is reported as 13.7. Reporting 14 throws away a decimal place the data support, and 13.67 or 13.666 claims more precision than the 0.3 mm reading has.
std
IV.B.4
A lab procedure rounds by the round-half-to-even rule. Readings of 3.45 and 3.55 are rounded to one decimal place. What are the results?
Under round-half-to-even, an exact 5 rounds to the nearest even digit, so 3.45 becomes 3.4 and 3.55 becomes 3.6. Getting 3.5 and 3.6 applies the round-half-up rule the procedure does not use.
std
IV.B.4
A value of −0.0023476 must be reported to three significant figures. What is the result?
The first three significant digits are 2, 3 and 4; the next digit is 7, so the magnitude rounds up to 0.00235 and the sign is kept. −0.00234 truncates instead of rounding.
std
IV.B.4
A specification limit is 2.5 maximum, and the procedure says to round results (half up) to the limit's decimal places before comparing. Readings are 2.54, 2.46 and 2.55. How many conform?
One
Three
None
Two
Rounded to one decimal place, 2.54 and 2.46 become 2.5 and conform, while 2.55 becomes 2.6 and does not. Comparing the raw readings would wrongly reject 2.54 under this stated rounding method.
std
IV.B.4
A technician must compute a result from several measured values. When should rounding be done?
After each step, to keep the numbers easy to work with
Before any calculation, to match the instrument display
Once, on the final result, keeping extra digits in the steps
Never, since all digits shown by the calculator are valid
Rounding at each step lets small errors pile up, so extra digits are carried and only the final result is rounded. Reporting every calculator digit overstates the precision of the data.
std
IV.B.5
An inch drawing specifies 1.250 ±0.005 in. What is the equivalent in millimeters?
Multiply both the size and the tolerance by 25.4: 1.250 × 25.4 = 31.750 and 0.005 × 25.4 = 0.127. Dividing by 25.4 instead gives 49.213, which goes the wrong way.
std
IV.B.5
A metric drawing specifies 50.00 +0/−0.05 mm. The inspector's gauge reads in inches. What inch limits apply?

50.00 ÷ 25.4 = 1.96850 in and 49.95 ÷ 25.4 = 1.96654 in, which round to 1.9685 and 1.9665 in. Where a converted limit must never widen the tolerance, the lower limit is rounded inward to 1.9666 in. Making the tolerance bilateral or flipping its direction changes the requirement, so both limits must be converted as written.
std
IV.B.5
A lab must hold 68 ±2 °F. Its thermometer reads 21.5 °C. What is the reading in °F, and is the lab in limits?
70.7 °F, so the room is above its limit
38.7 °F, so the room is below its limit
43.9 °F, so the room is below its limit
69.5 °F, so the room is within its limit
°F = °C × 1.8 + 32 = 21.5 × 1.8 + 32 = 70.7 °F, above the 70 °F upper limit. 38.7 °F forgets to add 32.
std
IV.B.5
A package spec says 2.5 kg maximum. The scale reads in pounds (1 lb = 0.4536 kg). What is the limit in pounds?
Pounds = kilograms ÷ 0.4536, so 2.5 ÷ 0.4536 = 5.51 lb. Multiplying by 0.4536 gives 1.13 lb, which converts in the wrong direction.
std
IV.B.5
A surface finish requirement is Ra 32 µin. What is it in micrometers?
813 µm
One microinch is 0.0254 µm, so 32 × 0.0254 = 0.81 µm. Dividing by 25.4 gives 1.26 µm, the wrong direction.
std
IV.B.5
A test requires a pressure of 150 psi (1 psi = 6.895 kPa). What is the test pressure in kPa?
21.8 kPa
1034 kPa
150 × 6.895 = 1034 kPa. Dividing by the factor gives 21.8 kPa; 10.34 is the value in bar, not kPa.
std
IV.B.5
A fastener torque is 25 N·m (1 N·m = 0.7376 lbf·ft). What is the torque in lbf·ft?
33.9 lbf·ft
18.4 lbf·ft
11.3 lbf·ft
2.5 lbf·ft
25 × 0.7376 = 18.4 lbf·ft. 33.9 lbf·ft results from dividing by the factor, which converts the wrong way.
std
IV.B.5
A pad area must be at least 2.00 in². What is that in mm²?
1290 mm²
50.8 mm²
2580 mm²
12.9 mm²
An area converts by the square of the length factor: 25.4² = 645.16, so 2.00 × 645.16 = 1290 mm². Using 25.4 once gives 50.8, which treats area like length.
std
IV.B.5
A cavity volume is 500 cm³ (1 in³ = 16.387 cm³). What is it in cubic inches?
8194 in³
19.7 in³
30.5 in³
500 ÷ 16.387 = 30.5 in³. Multiplying by the factor gives 8194 in³, and dividing by 25.4 or 2.54 treats volume like length.
std
IV.B.6
Bar stock arrives from a supplier that has never shipped to the plant before. Where should it first be checked?
At final inspection, once parts are made from it
At in-process inspection after the first machining
At first-article inspection of the finished part
At receiving, before release to stock
Receiving inspection verifies purchased material before it is used, which matters most when a supplier has no history. Waiting until final inspection lets value be added to material that may be bad.
std
IV.B.6
A large custom casting would cost thousands to ship back if rejected on arrival. Which inspection point fits best?
Receiving inspection on its arrival at the plant
Final inspection after it has been machined
Source inspection at the supplier
In-process inspection at the next operation

Source inspection verifies product at the supplier's site, so problems are fixed there instead of after costly freight. Receiving inspection would catch the problem only after the shipping cost is spent.
std
IV.B.6
An internal bore is covered by a pressed-in bushing in a later step and cannot be measured afterward. When should the bore be inspected?
At final inspection of the assembly
Before the bushing is installed
At receiving, on the raw casting
At the customer site after delivery
Characteristics that become inaccessible must be checked in process at the last point they can be reached. After assembly the bore can no longer be measured, so final inspection cannot verify it.
std
IV.B.6
Before releasing finished pumps to shipping, a plant runs a pressure test and checks the nameplate and packaging. Which inspection point is this?
Final inspection
In-process inspection
Source inspection
Receiving inspection

Final inspection confirms that the finished product, including its marking and packaging, meets requirements before release. In-process checks occur during manufacture, before the product is complete.
std
IV.B.6
A new injection mold has just been qualified, and the first parts come off the press. What inspection is most appropriate?
A full first-article layout of every drawing characteristic
A check of the critical dimensions only, then release
A visual check of the first part for flash and color
A receiving check of the raw resin certificate

First-article inspection verifies all drawing requirements on the first part from a new process, tool or design change before production runs. Checking only critical dimensions could miss a tooling error on another feature.
std
IV.B.6
A machine shop has been producing a part for years. Which event most clearly calls for a new first-article inspection?
Starting a new shift with the same operator team
Receiving a new lot of raw material from the same supplier
Reaching the end of the month's production run
Moving production of the part to a different machine
A new first article is triggered by changes that could affect conformance, such as new tooling, equipment, location or design revision. A routine new lot or shift is covered by normal inspection.
std
IV.B.6
A heat-treated shaft gets a surface hardness check, then is ground and plated. Where should the hardness check take place?
After plating, once the shaft is complete
At receiving, before any work is done on it
Right after heat treatment
At the customer, as part of acceptance testing

Checking right after heat treatment catches a bad batch before more value is added and before plating can mask the surface. Checking only at the end wastes grinding and plating on parts that may be scrap.
std
IV.B.6
A supplier has a long record of conforming lots and sends a certificate with each one. What is a reasonable change to receiving inspection?
Stop it entirely, since the certificate is enough
Reduce it and verify periodically
Increase it, since problems are now overdue
Move it to final inspection of the finished product
A proven supplier history justifies reduced receiving inspection, but periodic verification confirms the record still holds. Stopping all checks leaves no way to detect a change at the supplier.
std
IV.B.7
Two inspectors read the same analog dial gauge and get different results. One reads standing to the side of the dial. What error is most likely?
Fatigue
Parallax
Hysteresis
Cosine error

Parallax is the apparent shift of a pointer when read from an angle; reading square to the dial removes it. Cosine error comes from an indicator stem set at an angle to the measuring direction, not from the viewer's position.
std
IV.B.7
Audit data show that visual inspectors miss more defects in the last two hours of a ten-hour shift. What is the best response?
Add breaks and rotate tasks
Add a second visual check at the end of the line
Increase the line speed to shorten the shift
Tell inspectors to concentrate harder at the end
Fatigue lowers detection over time, so breaks and task rotation keep attention up. Adding a second tired inspector does little, and urging concentration does not change the cause.
std
IV.B.7
A 200 mm aluminum part (α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ /°C) is measured at 28 °C. How much longer is it than at the 20 °C reference temperature?
About 0.005 mm
About 0.129 mm
About 0.018 mm
About 0.037 mm
ΔL = L × α × ΔT = 200 × 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 8 = 0.037 mm. Using 28 °C instead of the 8 °C difference gives 0.129 mm, and leaving out ΔT gives 0.005 mm.
std
IV.B.7
A CMM is installed next to a stamping press, and its readings jump each time the press cycles. What is the most likely cause?
Humidity in the inspection room
Parallax when reading the screen
Floor vibration
Wear on the probe stylus tip
Readings that change in step with the press point to vibration, which is fixed by isolation or relocation. Stylus wear would cause a steady error, not one that follows the press cycle.
std
IV.B.7
Nylon parts measured right after molding pass, but the same parts fail after weeks in a damp warehouse. What is the most likely cause?
The gauge drifted out of calibration while idle
The inspector read the scale from an angle
The nylon absorbed moisture and changed size
The warehouse vibration loosened the parts
Nylon is hygroscopic and swells as it absorbs moisture, so humidity changes its dimensions. Gauge drift would affect all parts measured, not just ones stored in humid conditions.
std
IV.B.7
An inspector uses a vernier caliper with 0.02 mm resolution to check a ±0.005 mm tolerance. What kind of inspection error does this create?
Operator error, because the inspector is reading from an angle
Equipment error, because the gauge cannot discriminate the tolerance
Environment error, because the room temperature is too high
Setup error, because the caliper was not zeroed first

The caliper's resolution is coarser than the whole tolerance band, so it cannot tell good parts from bad no matter how carefully it is used. This is an equipment limitation, not an operator or environment problem.
std
IV.B.7
A dial indicator's plunger is set at an angle to the surface being measured instead of in line with the movement. What error results?
Cosine error that makes readings larger than the true movement
Cosine error that makes readings smaller than the true movement
Parallax error that depends on where the reader stands
Hysteresis error that appears only when direction reverses

With the plunger tilted, the surface moves the plunger farther than its own movement, so readings are larger. This is a setup error and is avoided by aligning the plunger with the direction of movement.
std
IV.B.7
An inspector zeros a comparator on a gauge block stack, but one block in the stack is the wrong size. What kind of error results?
A random error that averages out over many readings
A fatigue error that grows toward the end of the shift
An environment error that changes with room temperature
A setup error that shifts every reading by the same amount
Zeroing on the wrong master offsets every following reading by the same amount, which is a systematic setup error. It does not average out, because it is the same on every reading.
std
IV.B.7
A micrometer's anvils are worn so they no longer close flat and parallel. What effect will this have?
Readings are always too large by a fixed amount
Readings depend on the angle the user reads from
Readings are fine because the zero can be reset
Readings depend on the contact point
Worn, nonparallel anvils give readings that depend on where the part sits, an equipment limitation that resetting zero cannot correct. Viewing angle relates to parallax, not anvil condition.
std
IV.B.8
A steel supplier reports that one heat of material had low tensile strength. Which plant record lets the plant find every affected part quickly?
The supplier's latest quality certificate on file
The purchase order history for steel over the year
Records linking each work order to the heat numbers used
The final inspection reports for each part number
Traceability depends on recording which heat or lot went into each job, so a bad heat can be traced forward to the affected parts. Purchase history shows what was bought, not where each heat went.
std
IV.B.8
A lot of 1,000 castings is split into two jobs of 600 and 400 for different machining lines. How should identity be kept?
Keep the parent lot number on only the larger sublot
Link each sublot ID to the parent lot
Assign new, unrelated lot numbers to both sublots
Record the split only when one sublot has a problem
When a lot is split, each part must still trace to the original lot, so sublot IDs are linked to the parent. Unrelated new numbers break the chain back to the material's origin.
std
IV.B.8
During cleanup an operator finds a bin of fasteners with no tag and no record of their lot. What should be done?
Treat them as nonconforming until they can be identified
Return them to stock with the most recent lot number
Use them on non-critical jobs where traceability is less vital
Mix them into the next lot of the same part number
Once identity is lost, conformance and origin cannot be shown, so the material must be held as nonconforming. Assigning a guessed lot number creates a false record.
std
IV.B.8
A machining step removes the lot number stamped on a part's face. What is the best way to keep traceability?
Re-mark it or keep it with its traveler
Record the lot number after final inspection from memory
Rely on the drawing number, which is shared by all lots
Accept that the part is no longer traceable after machining
Identity must be transferred before the original marking is removed, either by re-marking or by keeping the part physically with its traveler. A drawing number identifies the design, not the lot.
std
IV.B.8
A customer reports a field failure on a serial-numbered valve. What does good traceability allow the plant to do?
Avoid any further investigation into the cause
Replace every valve ever shipped to the customer
Change the drawing so the failure cannot recur
Trace its build records and find similar units

Traceability links the serial number to its materials, operators, equipment and test records, so the cause can be found and the scope of any recall limited. Without it, the plant may have to recall far more product than needed.
std
IV.B.9
What does a certificate of compliance (CoC) normally provide?
Actual test results for the lot against each specification
A record of the calibration status of the supplier's gauges
A signed statement that the product meets the stated requirements
An approval from the customer to ship nonconforming product
A CoC is a supplier's attestation that product conforms, usually without the measured data. Reporting actual lot test results is what a certificate of analysis does.
std
IV.B.9
What does a certificate of analysis (CoA) provide that a CoC usually does not?
A signed promise that the product will meet requirements
Measured results for the lot, such as chemistry or tensile values
A list of the supplier's approved subcontractors
The supplier's quality system registration number
A CoA reports actual test results for the specific lot against specification limits. A signed statement of conformance without data is what a CoC gives.
std
IV.B.9
A CoA for a resin lot shows a melt flow index of 14.2. The purchase spec is 10 to 14. What should the receiving inspector do?
Accept the lot because a certificate was provided
Hold the lot as nonconforming and report it
Accept the lot because 14.2 rounds to 14
Return the CoA to the supplier for correction

The certificate itself shows a value outside the spec, so the lot must be held and handled as nonconforming. Having a certificate is not acceptance, and rounding to make a value pass is not allowed unless the spec states that method.
std
IV.B.9
A plant accepts castings on the supplier's CoA alone. What practice best confirms the certificates can be trusted?
Periodic in-house tests compared to the CoA
Check that each CoA is signed and dated by the supplier
Ask the supplier to switch from CoAs to CoCs
File the CoAs and review them only after a complaint
Periodic independent testing checks that the supplier's reported results match reality. A signature shows who issued the certificate, not that its data are accurate.
std
IV.C.1
A single sampling plan is n = 50, Ac = 1, Re = 2. The sample contains 2 defective units. What is the decision?
Accept the lot
Take a second sample of 50
Accept the lot on tightened inspection
Reject the lot
The number of defectives equals the rejection number, so the lot is rejected. A second sample applies only to double or multiple sampling plans.
std
IV.C.1
A lot is accepted under a plan of n = 80, Ac = 2. One defective was found in the sample. What should happen to that defective unit?
Ship it with the lot, since the lot was accepted
Reject the whole lot, since a defective was found
Remove or replace it before shipment
Return it to the lot, since it is within the AQL
Accepting a lot does not make known defectives acceptable; nonconforming units found in the sample are removed or replaced. Rejecting the lot ignores the plan, which allows up to two defectives.
std
IV.C.1
Under ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 normal inspection, the last five lots were accepted, rejected, accepted, accepted, rejected. What should happen next?
Stay on normal inspection
Switch to reduced inspection
Switch to tightened inspection
Stop inspection until corrective action
The switching rule moves from normal to tightened when two of five or fewer consecutive lots are not accepted. Discontinuing inspection applies only after continued rejections while on tightened.
std
IV.C.1
A product has been on tightened inspection under ANSI/ASQ Z1.4. What is required to return to normal inspection?
Two consecutive lots accepted on original inspection
Five consecutive lots accepted
Ten consecutive lots accepted with no defectives
A supplier request with a corrective action plan
The standard returns to normal when five consecutive lots are accepted on tightened inspection. Ten lots relates to the conditions for moving to reduced inspection, not back from tightened.
std
IV.C.1
Under a standard AQL scheme, the lot size increases from 500 to 5,000 units at the same inspection level and AQL. What happens to the sample size?
It increases, but by much less than ten times
It stays the same
It increases by exactly ten times, like the lot
It decreases, since larger lots are more uniform

Sample size grows with lot size in AQL schemes, but much less than proportionally, because protection depends mainly on sample size, not on the fraction sampled. Keeping it fixed ignores the lot size step in finding the code letter.
std
IV.C.1
What do the acceptance number (Ac) and rejection number (Re) of a single sampling plan represent?
The fewest defectives allowed to accept, and the most allowed to reject
The share of the lot to inspect, and the share allowed to be defective
The number of lots to accept before reducing, and before tightening
The most defectives allowed to accept, and the fewest that force rejection

Ac is the largest number of defectives (or defects) in the sample that still allows acceptance; Re, usually Ac + 1 in single sampling, is the smallest number that requires rejection. Switching between levels is decided by separate rules.
std
IV.C.2
A plant samples a fixed 10% of every lot, whatever its size. What is the main weakness of this practice?
It gives the same protection on every lot, which wastes time
It cannot be used with attributes data from go/no-go gauges
It requires the data to follow a normal distribution
Protection varies with lot size

Sampling protection depends mainly on sample size, so 10% of a small lot gives little protection and 10% of a large lot is costly. A statistically designed plan gives defined protection at each lot size.
std
IV.C.2
A double sampling plan is n₁ = 32, Ac₁ = 1, Re₁ = 4; n₂ = 32, Ac₂ = 4, Re₂ = 5. The first sample has 2 defectives and the second has 1. What is the decision?
Reject, because the first sample exceeded Ac₁ = 1
Reject, because the total of 3 exceeds Ac₁ = 1
Accept, because the total of 3 is within Ac₂ = 4
Take a third sample, because the result is unclear
Two defectives fall between Ac₁ and Re₁, so a second sample is taken; the cumulative count of 3 is at or below Ac₂ = 4, so the lot is accepted. Exceeding Ac₁ alone only triggers the second sample.
std
IV.C.2
What is the main advantage of a double sampling plan over a single sampling plan with similar protection?
The second sample makes acceptance of bad lots impossible
Very good or very bad lots are often decided on the smaller first sample
The plan is simpler to train and to administer on the floor
The plan always inspects fewer units than a single plan
Double sampling can decide clearly good or bad lots on the first sample, lowering the average amount inspected. It is more complex to run, and some lots need more total units than the single plan.
std
IV.C.2
A supplier has shipped many consecutive lots that all passed inspection. The plant now inspects only one lot in four, chosen at random. What is this called?
Skip-lot sampling
Reduced inspection
Double sampling
Fixed sampling
Skip-lot sampling inspects only a fraction of lots once a supplier has shown sustained good quality. Reduced inspection still samples every lot, just with a smaller sample.
std
IV.C.2
A plant moves a critical safety feature to 100% visual inspection. Why might some defects still escape?
Manual 100% inspection suffers from fatigue
Every unit is checked, so no defects can be missed by design
Sampling plans always find more defects than 100% checks do
Visual inspection cannot be used on any safety features at all
Manual 100% inspection is often well short of 100% effective, because attention drops with repetition. That is why automated or error-proofed checks are preferred for critical features.
std
IV.C.2
Compared with an attributes plan, what is a main advantage of a variables sampling plan?
It can cover many characteristics with one plan
It needs no assumption about the data's distribution
It can be used with go/no-go gauges on the line
It gives similar protection with a smaller sample

Measured values carry more information than pass or fail, so variables plans need fewer units for similar protection. They do, however, require a separate plan for each characteristic and usually assume normality.
std
IV.C.2
A product has eight characteristics checked with go/no-go gauges. Which sampling approach fits best?
A variables plan for each of the eight characteristics
A variables plan that uses the average of all eight
An attributes plan counting defectives
No sampling, since go/no-go gauges need 100% checks
Go/no-go gauges give pass or fail results, which suit an attributes plan, and one plan can cover several characteristics. Variables plans need measured values and a separate plan per characteristic.
std
IV.C.2
What is the purpose of acceptance sampling?
To estimate the exact defect rate of a lot
To decide whether to accept or reject a lot
To control the process while parts are made
To improve quality by inspecting more parts
Acceptance sampling is a lot-sentencing tool: it decides the fate of a lot. It does not control or improve the process, and its samples are not meant to give a precise estimate of lot quality.
std
IV.C.2
Of 40,000 parts shipped last quarter, 12 were found defective by the customer. What is the defect rate in parts per million?
300 PPM
30 PPM
333 PPM
PPM = 12 ÷ 40,000 × 1,000,000 = 300. 3,000 or 30 come from misplacing the decimal point by a factor of ten.
std
IV.C.2

Incoming lots are 2% defective, and the sampling plan accepts 60% of such lots. Rejected lots are fully screened and defectives replaced. Lot size is large compared with the sample. What is the approximate AOQ?
AOQ ≈ p × Pa = 0.02 × 0.60 = 0.012, or 1.2%, because screened rejected lots leave with no defectives. 0.8% uses the probability of rejection instead of acceptance.
std
IV.C.2
Under rectifying inspection, why does average outgoing quality improve again when incoming quality becomes very poor?
The sample size grows automatically as quality worsens
Poor lots have fewer units, so fewer defectives reach the customer
Suppliers stop shipping once their lots begin to fail
Most lots are rejected and screened, so few defectives get through
When incoming quality is very poor, most lots are rejected and 100% screened, which removes their defectives. That is why the AOQ curve rises to a maximum, the AOQL, and then falls.
std
IV.C.2
In a single sampling plan, what decides the lot's fate?
The number of defectives in two samples taken in a row
The percentage of lots accepted over the last month
Defectives in one sample versus Ac and Re
The number of units inspected until a defective is found
A single plan takes one sample and compares the result with the acceptance and rejection numbers. Taking a second sample when results are unclear is what defines double sampling.
std
IV.C.3
Under an ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 style scheme, what determines the sample size code letter?
The AQL and the number of defects found
The lot size and the AQL selected
The lot size and the inspection level
The inspection level and the AQL selected
The code letter comes from lot size and inspection level; the AQL is then used with the code letter to find n, Ac and Re. The AQL does not affect which code letter applies.
std
IV.C.3
What does an AQL of 1.0% mean for a supplier's process?
It allows 1% of every shipped lot to be defective by contract
It is the poorest process average that is acceptable for sampling purposes
It guarantees that accepted lots are at most 1% defective
It is the defect rate at which lots are always rejected

The AQL is the worst tolerable process average for acceptance sampling; lots at that level are accepted most of the time. It does not guarantee the quality of any single lot, and it is not permission to ship defectives.
std
IV.C.3
A test destroys each unit and is costly. Which choice of inspection level is most suitable?
A special level such as S-2
General level III to get the most protection
General level II because it is the usual default
No level, since destructive tests cannot be sampled
The special inspection levels give small samples for costly or destructive tests, accepting more sampling risk. Level III would increase the number of units destroyed.
std
IV.C.3
A lot of 1,200 molded parts came from three cavities: 600 from cavity 1, 400 from cavity 2 and 200 from cavity 3. A sample of 60 is taken in proportion. How many come from each cavity?
Proportional stratified sampling takes 60 × 600/1,200 = 30, 60 × 400/1,200 = 20 and 60 × 200/1,200 = 10. Taking 20 from each over-samples the smallest cavity.
std
IV.C.3
Parts arrive in a crate of ten layered trays. The operator samples all units from the top tray because it is easiest. What is the problem?
The sample size is too large for a crate
The top tray is always the worst quality
Layered trays cannot be sampled at all
It may not represent the lot

Convenience samples from one location can miss problems elsewhere in the lot; units should be drawn at random from all trays. There is no rule that the top tray is worse, which is exactly why it cannot stand for the lot.
std
IV.C.3
Which method gives every unit in a lot of 500 numbered parts an equal chance of being selected?
Take every part from the first box opened
Have the inspector choose parts that look typical
Select by random numbers
Take the last 20 parts produced in the run
Random selection by random numbers gives each unit the same chance of selection. Inspector choice brings in bias, even with good intentions.
std
IV.C.3
A plan for a lot of 3,000 calls for n = 125, Ac = 3, Re = 4. The sample has 3 defectives. What is the decision?
Reject the lot, since the defectives exceed 2%
Accept the lot and handle the 3 defectives
Take a second sample before deciding
Reject the lot, since any defect is too many
Three defectives equals Ac, so the lot is accepted, and the three defective units are removed or replaced. The decision follows the plan's Ac and Re, not a percentage judged afterward.
std
IV.C.3
An inspector finds a critical defect in a sample from a lot whose plan has Ac = 0 for critical defects. What should she do?
Reject the lot, since the critical acceptance number is zero
Accept the lot if the major and minor counts are within limits
Take a larger sample to see if the defect repeats
Accept the lot and note the defect on the report
With Ac = 0, one critical defect means rejection, whatever the counts for other classes. Each defect class is judged against its own criteria.
std
IV.D.1
An inspector finds a bore 0.01 mm over its upper limit. She believes the part will still work. What should she do?
Identify it as nonconforming and send it for review
Accept it, since the part will work in the assembly
Rework it herself before anyone else sees it
Re-measure until she gets a reading in tolerance

The inspector's role is to judge conformance to requirements; whether a nonconforming part can be used is decided by the authorized review process. Re-measuring until a passing number appears falsifies the result.
std
IV.D.1
What should a tag on rejected material include, at minimum?
The part number and a red color, with details kept in a notebook
The disposition decided by the inspector at the time of rejection
The name of the operator to blame for the nonconformance
Part, lot, defect, quantity, date and inspector

A reject tag must identify the material and its problem clearly enough that anyone can tell what it is and why it is held. Disposition is decided later by the review authority, not set on the tag by the inspector.
std
IV.D.1
Rejected parts are tagged. Where should they be kept until disposition?
On the line next to good parts, with the tags attached
In the scrap bin, so no one can use them by mistake
In a controlled hold area
In the shipping area, ready to go back to the supplier
Physical segregation in a controlled area prevents accidental use while the material awaits disposition. Scrapping or shipping before review removes the chance to decide on rework, use or return.
std
IV.D.1
A rejected welded frame is too large to move to the hold cage. What is the best way to segregate it?
Leave it in place without a tag until the MRB meets
Tag it and barricade it in place
Cut it up so it fits into the hold cage
Move it to the end of the line with the good frames
When material cannot be moved, segregation is done in place by tagging and barricading or marking the area. Cutting it up would destroy options for disposition such as repair or use as is.
std
IV.D.1
What should a nonconformance report (NCR) record about the problem?
Only the part number, so the review board can investigate
The requirement, the actual condition found and how much material is affected
The inspector's opinion of whether the part can be used
The corrective action that has already been taken on the process
An NCR records what was required, what was found and the scope, so reviewers can decide disposition and corrective action. Opinions on usability are for the review, not the record of the defect.
std
IV.D.1
An inspector finds that red reject tags have been removed from a hold pallet, and the parts have been mixed with stock. What should she do?
Hold the whole mixed lot as suspect
Pull out the parts she remembers seeing tagged
Release the parts, since the tags are now gone
Re-tag only the parts that look defective

Once rejected parts are mixed in, they cannot be told apart, so all affected material must be held until it is screened or dispositioned. Relying on memory or looks risks shipping nonconforming parts.
std
IV.D.1
A plant's ERP system controls shipping. What should be done in the system when a lot is rejected?
Leave the status unchanged until the MRB meets
Mark the lot as scrap so it is written off at once
Delete the lot so no one can find it in the system
Put the lot on hold status
An electronic hold supports the physical tag and stops the system from allowing use or shipment. Writing it off as scrap makes a disposition decision before review.
std
IV.D.2
What is the main function of a material review board (MRB)?
To approve the quality budget for each department
To audit suppliers before they are approved
To disposition nonconforming material
To set the AQL for every product produced

The MRB is a cross-functional group, usually quality and engineering, sometimes the customer, that reviews nonconforming material and decides what to do with it. Supplier approval and AQL setting are separate functions.
std
IV.D.2
Which group is most appropriate to serve on an MRB?
The inspector who found the nonconformance, alone
Purchasing and finance, to keep scrap costs down
Quality and engineering, plus customer if needed
The operators who made the nonconforming parts
MRB decisions need technical and quality authority, and the customer's input when a disposition affects their requirements. An inspector alone lacks authority to accept nonconforming product.
std
IV.D.2
Before an MRB can disposition a part as use as is, what must it determine?
That the cost of scrap would be higher than the cost of use
That form, fit, function and safety are unaffected
That the nonconformance is smaller than 10% of tolerance
That the operator who made the part has been retrained
Fitness for use means the nonconformance does not harm form, fit, function, safety, reliability or compliance, which needs engineering evaluation. Cost alone does not make a part fit for use.
std
IV.D.2
An MRB decides a customer-specified dimension can be used as is. When is the customer's approval normally needed?
When it departs from a customer requirement
Only when the MRB members cannot agree on a vote
Never, since the MRB has final authority on all parts
Only when the parts are scrapped instead of used

When product does not meet a customer or contract requirement, use as is or repair normally requires the customer's concession. The MRB's internal authority does not extend to waiving the customer's requirements.
std
IV.D.2
How does rework differ from repair?
Repair restores full conformance; rework makes the part usable but still nonconforming
Rework is done by the supplier; repair is done by the customer after delivery
Rework applies to assemblies only; repair applies to single parts only
Rework restores full conformance; repair makes the part usable but still nonconforming

Rework brings the product into full conformance with original requirements, while repair makes it acceptable for its intended use without fully meeting them. That is why repair usually needs a concession and rework does not.
std
IV.D.2
Shafts that were oversize are reground to bring them within the drawing tolerance. What must happen before they are released?
Release them as reworked
Ask the customer to sign a concession for each shaft
Mark them as repaired and ship them separately
Reinspect them to the original requirements
Reworked product must be reverified to confirm it now conforms. A concession is not needed for rework, because the product meets the original requirements once verified.
std
IV.D.2
A supplier's bearings have the wrong seal type and cannot be used or reworked in-house. Which disposition fits best?
Use as is under a deviation
Repair by changing the seals
Return to supplier
Rework in the plant
Purchased material that cannot be used or corrected is usually returned to the supplier for replacement or credit. Use as is would install the wrong seal, which affects function.
std
IV.D.2
A batch of cracked castings cannot be repaired and has no other use. What disposition should the MRB give, and what follows?
Scrap them, and return the good portions to stock for use
Scrap them and control their destruction
Use them as is, since cracks are hard to see in the field
Hold them in the cage until the next MRB review cycle

Scrap is the disposition when material cannot be made usable, and it must be controlled or destroyed so it cannot reenter production. Leaving it on hold indefinitely delays the decision without reducing risk.
std
IV.D.2
The MRB has dispositioned the same nonconformance on the same part three months in a row. What should it do next?
Request corrective action to remove the root cause
Keep dispositioning it, since the parts are being used
Raise the tolerance so the parts will conform
Stop reviewing it and accept the parts by default
Disposition deals with the material; recurring nonconformances need corrective action on the cause. Changing the tolerance without an engineering basis hides the problem.
std
V.A
Trained auditors employed by a plant examine the plant's own receiving process against company procedures. How is this audit best described?
An internal, first-party audit
A second-party audit by the plant
