A third-party compliance audit
An external certification audit
An organization auditing itself with its own people is an internal, or first-party, audit. It becomes second-party only when a customer (or someone acting for one) audits a supplier.
std
V.A
Which of these is an external audit of a contract molder?
The molder's own lead auditor audits shipping for the molder's plant manager
The molder's customer sends a supplier quality engineer to audit its molding process
A corporate auditor from a sister division audits the molder under its internal program
The molder's quality manager reviews last quarter's internal audit results with staff

An external audit is performed by a party outside the organization, such as a customer or a certification body. A corporate auditor working under the company's own internal program is still doing a first-party audit, even if he comes from another division.
std
V.A
An auditor checks whether a company's quality management system as a whole meets each clause of ISO 9001, sampling evidence in several departments. What type of audit is this?
Product audit
Process audit
Systems audit
Virtual audit

A systems audit evaluates the management system as a whole against a standard such as ISO 9001. A process audit looks in depth at one process and its controls, not at every clause across the organization.
std
V.A
An auditor pulls five packed cartons from the shipping dock after they have passed final inspection and checks them against the drawing, label and packaging requirements. What type of audit is this?
A process audit of final inspection
A systems audit of shipping
A first-article inspection
A product audit

A product audit examines finished product, usually after inspection, to confirm it meets requirements from the customer's point of view. A process audit would focus on how the inspection or packing process is run and controlled, not on re-checking the product itself.
std
V.A

On a heat-treat line, an auditor compares furnace temperature, time at temperature, operator training records and the quench procedure with the process specification. What type of audit is this mainly?
A process audit
A product audit
A systems audit
A third-party audit

Checking the inputs, controls, parameters and people of one operation against its specification is a process audit. A product audit would measure the heat-treated parts themselves, for example hardness, rather than the way they were processed.
std
V.A

Because travel is restricted, an auditor will review records shared on screen and watch the assembly line through a live video feed carried by a guide. Which planning step is most specific to this type of audit?
Drop the opening meeting, since the participants will not meet face to face
Test the connection, camera views and record access before the audit starts
Accept verbal statements in place of records, since documents cannot be handled
Limit the audit to procedures, since the line itself cannot be observed remotely

A virtual audit depends on technology working, so the team must confirm connectivity, camera coverage and access to records in advance. Opening meetings, records and observation all still apply in a remote audit; they are simply carried out through the technology.
std
V.A
Which statement best describes a virtual audit?
It is a self-assessment by the process owner, recorded on video for later review
It is a desk review of procedures done before any on-site audit is scheduled
It uses video and shared records to audit when being on site is impractical
It replaces the audit plan with an informal online talk between auditor and auditee

A virtual (remote) audit is a planned audit that uses information and communication technology, such as video and screen sharing, to collect evidence. It follows the same plan, criteria and evidence rules as an on-site audit; it is not a self-assessment or an informal discussion.
std
V.A
A medical device maker sends its supplier quality engineer to audit a contract molder that supplies it with housings. What type of audit is this?
A first-party audit
A third-party audit, because the auditor is from another company
A registrar audit
A second-party audit
A customer auditing its supplier is a second-party audit. It is not third-party, because a third party is independent of both the customer and the supplier, such as a certification body.
std
V.A
A plant hires an accredited registrar to assess its quality management system for ISO 9001 certification. Who performs this audit, and what type is it?
An independent certification body, so third-party
The plant's major customers, so it is second-party
The plant's internal audit team, so it is first-party
The plant's corporate office, so it is second-party
Certification audits are done by an independent body that has no stake as buyer or seller, which makes them third-party audits. Customer audits are second-party; they do not lead to certification.
std
V.A
Which of these is a first-party audit?
A government regulator inspects a pharmaceutical plant for compliance
A company audits its own calibration area using staff from purchasing
An automaker audits the welding process of one of its tier-one suppliers
A registrar performs an annual surveillance audit of a certified plant

First-party means the organization audits itself, even when auditors come from a different department. Regulator and registrar audits are third-party, and an automaker auditing a supplier is second-party.
std
V.A
A plant assigns internal auditors from departments other than the one being audited. What is the main reason?
To shorten the audit, since outsiders need less background on the area
To let the department's own supervisor act as the guide for the audit
To stay objective, since auditors should not audit their own work
To give the department time to fix problems before the auditors arrive
Independence from the work being audited protects objectivity, which is a basic principle for internal auditors. Outsiders usually need more preparation, not less, so saving time is not the reason.
std
V.B
Before an audit of a paint line, the lead auditor writes: "Determine whether the paint line's controls meet the customer's coating requirements." This statement defines the audit's:
Scope and boundaries
Reference criteria
Audit plan
Purpose (objective)
The purpose or objective states why the audit is being done and what it should determine. Scope sets the boundaries, such as which lines, shifts and activities are covered.
std
V.B
Which statement is an example of audit scope?
Paint line 2, both shifts, from part loading through final cure check
Verify that paint line 2 conforms to the customer's coating specification
Customer coating specification CS-14 and work instruction WI-220, revision C
Opening meeting at 8:00, line observation from 8:30 until 11:00, then records

Scope describes the extent and boundaries of the audit: locations, shifts, activities and time period. The other options are the objective, the criteria and the schedule, which are separate parts of audit planning.
std
V.B

An auditor writes a nonconformity stating that operators "should wear cut-resistant gloves," but he cannot point to any procedure, standard or customer requirement calling for gloves. What is the main problem?
The finding needs a photo before it can be accepted
The finding is not tied to any audit criterion
The finding should be graded major, as it involves safety
The finding should be addressed to the operators directly

A nonconformity is a failure to meet a requirement, so it must cite the reference standard or criterion that was not met. Without a requirement, the concern can at most be an observation, however important it seems.
std
V.B
For a process audit of a wire crimping operation, which item would serve as an audit reference standard?
The operator's view of the best crimp height for each wire size
The checklist questions the auditor wrote for this particular audit
The crimp height specification and the crimp press work instruction
Last year's audit report on the same crimping operation

Reference standards (criteria) are the requirements that evidence is compared against, such as specifications and procedures. A checklist is a tool the auditor uses to work through the criteria; it is not itself the requirement.
std
V.B
Which content belongs in the audit plan sent to the auditee before the audit?
A list of the nonconformities the team expects to find
The corrective actions the auditee must complete beforehand
The final grade the team plans to give each audited area
Dates, areas to visit, audit team, scope and criteria

The audit plan tells the auditee what will be audited, when, by whom and against what, so the right people and records are available. Findings and grades come from evidence gathered during the audit and cannot be decided in advance.
std
V.B
While preparing for a process audit, what should the auditor review to plan efficient fieldwork?
The process documents, prior audit results and open corrective actions for the area
The personnel files of each operator who is likely to be interviewed during the audit
The sections of the standard the auditor knows best, so the questions go quickly
The auditee's budget and staffing plans for next year, to judge future resources

Reviewing the area's documents, history and open actions shows the auditor what the process should do and where risk has appeared before. Picking topics the auditor is comfortable with skews coverage and is not a sound basis for planning.
std
V.B
An auditor schedules six processes at 1.5 hours each, plus a 0.5-hour opening meeting and a 0.5-hour closing meeting. How many hours should the audit plan allow?
9.0 hours
10.0 hours
9.5 hours
11.0 hours
Six processes at 1.5 hours is 9.0 hours, plus 0.5 + 0.5 hours of meetings gives 10.0 hours. Answering 9.0 hours leaves out both meetings, which are part of the audit and must be scheduled.
std
V.B
During an audit, an operator says, "We always check the first piece," but no first-piece records can be found for the last two weeks. The procedure requires those records. What should the auditor do?
Accept the statement, since the operator is the person who does the check
Stop the audit and report the operator to the supervisor for discipline
Seek other evidence of the check and record a finding if none exists
Mark the check as verified, because the procedure says it is required

A verbal claim is not objective evidence until it is confirmed by records or observation, and missing required records are themselves a gap. A procedure that requires a check does not prove the check happened.
std
V.B
Halfway through an audit, the auditor learns that a key area in the plan is shut down for maintenance. What is the best action?
Skip the area and report it as conforming in the final audit report
Review only that area's records and mark it as fully audited
Add a day to the audit without informing the auditee first
Tell the lead auditor and the auditee, and agree how to adjust the plan

Changes to the audit plan during performance should be communicated and agreed with the auditee and the lead auditor, and any unaudited area noted. Reporting an area as conforming or fully audited without the planned evidence misstates the audit.
std
V.B
Which is a main purpose of the opening meeting?
Confirm the plan, scope and schedule and how the audit will run
Present preliminary findings to the managers of the audited area
Assign corrective action owners for any problems expected
Decide which findings from the last audit can now be closed

The opening meeting confirms the plan, introduces the team and agrees logistics, communication and confidentiality before fieldwork starts. Findings are presented at the closing meeting, after evidence has been gathered.
std
V.B
At the closing meeting, the auditee's manager disagrees with a finding. What should the lead auditor do?
Withdraw the finding so that the meeting can end with everyone in full agreement
Review the evidence with her and record any unresolved disagreement
Upgrade the finding to major to make clear to the manager how serious it is
Postpone the closing meeting until the manager formally accepts the finding
Diverging opinions should be discussed and resolved where possible; if they are not, they are recorded. Dropping a finding that the evidence supports, just to avoid conflict, compromises the audit.
std
V.B
An auditor finds that a plant has no process for calibrating its gauges, and none of the 40 gauges sampled has a calibration record. How should this most likely be graded?
Minor nonconformity
Observation
Major nonconformity
Opportunity for improvement

The total absence of a required system element is a classic major nonconformity because it puts product conformance at risk. A minor nonconformity is an isolated lapse in a system that otherwise exists and works.
std
V.B

The training procedure requires a trainee signature on each completed training record. In a sample of 25 records, one is missing the signature; the other 24 are complete and the operator is shown to be competent. How should this be classified?
Major nonconformity
Observation only
No finding
Minor nonconformity
A single lapse against a stated requirement, in a system that is otherwise working, is a minor nonconformity. It is more than an observation because a documented requirement was not met.
std
V.B
An auditor notes that the gauge storage cabinet is almost full and gauges may soon be left on open benches, but no requirement is being violated today. How should this be reported?
As an observation of a potential concern
As a minor nonconformity against gauge storage
As a major nonconformity, given the risk to gauges
As a corrective action request to the supervisor
An observation records a potential problem or improvement point where no requirement has yet been broken. A nonconformity, major or minor, needs evidence that a requirement is not met.
std
V.B
Which content is most appropriate for the final audit report?
The names of operators who made errors, ranked by number of mistakes
Objectives, scope, criteria, findings with evidence, and conclusions
The auditor's personal opinions of each manager's leadership style
Every page of unedited interview notes taken during the audit

The report gives a complete, accurate and concise record of what was audited, against what, what was found and what was concluded. Blaming individuals or including raw notes and personal opinions does not belong in a factual audit report.
std
V.B
An auditee emails that the corrective action for a nonconformity is complete. What should the auditor do before closing it?
Close it based on the auditee's written statement that it is complete
Leave it open until next year's audit without any further contact
Confirm with evidence that the action was put in place and is working
Ask the auditee to score the action's effectiveness on a 1-to-5 scale
Closing a finding requires verifying, through records, a follow-up visit or both, that the action was implemented and was effective. An auditee's statement alone is not objective evidence of either.
std
V.B

Three months after an audit, an auditor checks that a corrective action for mislabeled bins was implemented and finds the new labels in place. What else should be confirmed before the nonconformity is closed?
That the auditee signed the original nonconformity report
That the labels were bought from an approved supplier
That the closing meeting minutes list the action owner
That bins checked since the change are labeled correctly

Verification covers both implementation and effectiveness, so the auditor should see evidence that labeling errors have not recurred. A signed report or meeting minutes shows administration, not that the problem was solved.
std
V.C
What is the main benefit of preparing an audit checklist?
It keeps the audit on scope and helps make sure key requirements are covered
It limits the auditor to the listed questions so no other issues are raised
It replaces the need to gather records, since answers are written on the list
It lets the auditee prepare answers in advance so the audit runs smoothly

A checklist organizes the audit, ties questions to criteria and helps ensure nothing important is missed. It is a guide, not a limit; auditors still follow up on issues they find that are not on the list.
std
V.C

During a process audit using a prepared checklist, an auditor sees an unlabeled container of solvent at a workstation in the audited area. The checklist does not mention chemical labeling. What should he do?
Ignore it, since only items on the checklist can produce audit findings
Follow up on it, since a checklist guides an audit without limiting it
Add it to next year's checklist and leave it out of this audit's report
Ask the auditee whether they would like it included in the audit report
Auditors use checklists as a guide and still pursue relevant evidence they observe within scope. Ignoring an obvious issue because it was not on the list defeats the purpose of the audit.
std
V.C
Which of these are audit working papers?
The auditee's procedures and work instructions for the area
The certificate issued after a successful certification audit
Checklists, sampling records, notes and interview records
The company's quality policy and its posted quality objectives

Working papers are the documents auditors create and use to plan, perform and record the audit, and they support the findings. The auditee's procedures are audit criteria or evidence sources, not the auditor's working papers.
std
V.C
Why should audit working papers be kept after the audit report is issued?
They replace the report if the auditee disputes its wording
They are given to operators as training on the audited process
They let the auditor rewrite findings after the closing meeting
They hold the evidence that supports the reported findings

Working papers are the record of what was examined and what was found, so they back up the findings if questions arise later. They support the report; they do not replace it or allow findings to be changed after the fact.
std
V.C
Which approach gives the auditor the strongest evidence that operators follow the machine setup procedure?
Watching several setups and comparing each step with the procedure
Asking the supervisor whether setups follow the written procedure
Reading the procedure to confirm it is approved, current and posted
Asking each operator to describe the procedure from memory

Direct observation of the activity, compared against the requirement, is strong first-hand evidence of practice. A supervisor's assurance is second-hand, and an approved procedure shows only what should happen, not what does.
std
V.C
Which item is objective evidence?
A supervisor's statement that inspection is always done on time
A dated inspection record of measured values for lot 2215
The auditor's impression that the whole area seems well run
An operator's estimate of how often gauges are checked

Objective evidence is verifiable data, such as records, observations or measurements, that shows something exists or is true. Statements, impressions and estimates are not objective evidence until they are confirmed.
std
V.C
A receiving supervisor tells the auditor that every incoming lot is inspected. How can this statement become objective evidence?
Have the supervisor sign a written statement saying it is true
Write it in the audit notes along with the supervisor's name
Confirm it with receiving records or by observation
Ask the supervisor's manager to approve the statement in writing

Interview statements must be verified by records, observation or measurement before they count as objective evidence. A signature or manager approval makes the claim more formal but does not prove inspection actually took place.
std
V.C
An auditor starts with a customer order and follows it through order review, production planning, manufacturing, inspection and shipping. What technique is this?
Backward tracing
Stratified sampling
Process mapping
Forward tracing
Forward tracing follows the flow of work from its start, here the order, through to the output. Backward tracing runs the other way, from a finished product or record back to its inputs.
std
V.C
An auditor picks a finished assembly from the warehouse and works back through its inspection records, build records, material certificates and receiving records. What does this technique test best?
Traceability from product back to its inputs
Whether every new order is reviewed before it is accepted
Whether the purchasing process selects suppliers properly
Whether the production schedule is met each week

Backward tracing starts with an output and follows the records chain back to raw material, which tests traceability directly. Order review and supplier selection are better tested by following work forward from where it starts.
std
V.C
In which situation is backward tracing the best choice?
Checking that new purchase orders are reviewed before release
Investigating a field failure on serial number 4471
Following a new hire's training from start to sign-off
Confirming that incoming lots are logged when they arrive

When the starting point is a specific failed or finished unit, tracing backward through its history is the natural way to find where things went wrong. The other situations start at the beginning of a process and suit forward tracing.
std
V.C

An audit program procedure says to sample 10% of the records in a population, with a minimum of 5 records. A department has 38 maintenance work orders for the period. How many should the auditor sample?
3 records
4 records
5 records
38 records
Ten percent of 38 is 3.8, which rounds to 4, but the procedure sets a minimum of 5, so 5 records are sampled. Answering 4 applies the percentage and overlooks the minimum.
std
V.C
An auditor randomly selects 12 of 240 batch records and finds 2 missing a required signature. What percentage of the sample is nonconforming?
Two of the 12 records sampled is 2 ÷ 12 = 16.7%. Dividing by the population, 2 ÷ 240 = 0.83%, wrongly assumes the other 228 records are all conforming.
std
V.C
Why should an auditor pick audit samples herself rather than let the auditee choose them?
The auditee may pick its best records and hide problems
Auditor-chosen samples need fewer records to support a conclusion
Auditor selection removes the need to read the governing procedure
Auditee-chosen samples cannot be recorded in the working papers

Samples chosen by the auditee can be biased toward good results, so random or auditor-controlled selection keeps the sample representative. Who chooses the sample does not change how many records are needed.
std
V.C

The audit program procedure requires auditors to cover at least two shifts when auditing a process that runs around the clock. An auditor can reach only day shift during her visit. What should she do?
Treat day shift as typical and report all shifts as covered
Tell the lead auditor and record the limitation
Drop the process from the audit without noting it anywhere
Ask a day-shift operator to describe the night-shift practices

Procedural guidelines set out how audits are to be done; when one cannot be followed, the deviation and its effect on coverage must be reported and recorded. Reporting coverage that was not achieved misstates the audit.
std
V.C
Why does an organization issue procedural guidelines for its audit program?
So each auditor can choose a personal method for every audit
So the auditee can approve the findings before they are issued
So audits are planned, sampled and reported consistently
So audits can skip the opening and closing meetings when busy

Audit procedures give all auditors common rules for planning, sampling, evidence, grading and reporting, which makes results consistent and comparable. Leaving methods to personal choice is exactly what such guidelines are meant to avoid.
std
VI.A
An X-bar chart for a shaft diameter uses subgroups of n = 5. The grand average is 25.000 mm and the average range is 0.40 mm. With A2 = 0.577, what are the control limits?
The limits are 25.000 ± A2 × R-bar = 25.000 ± 0.577 × 0.40 = 25.000 ± 0.231 mm. Using ± R-bar alone gives 24.600 to 25.400 mm, which ignores the A2 constant.
std
VI.A
All points on an X-bar chart are inside the control limits, but the last eight points have risen steadily toward the upper limit. How should this be treated?
As a likely special cause to investigate before parts drift out of specification
As an in-control process needing no action until a point exceeds a limit
As a reason to widen the control limits so the chart reflects the new level
As normal variation, since the points remain inside the control limits

A steady run in one direction is a nonrandom pattern that signals a likely special cause, such as tool wear, even with no point outside the limits. Waiting for an out-of-limit point gives up the early warning that makes trend analysis useful for managing risk.
std
VI.A
A team lists the ways a torque operation could fail, the effect of each failure on the customer, likely causes and the current controls, and then rates each. Which tool are they using?
Design FMEA
Process FMEA
Control plan
Fault tree
A PFMEA examines how a manufacturing or assembly step can fail and what controls exist. A DFMEA looks at how the product design itself could fail to meet its function.
std
VI.A
Which failure mode belongs in a design FMEA rather than a process FMEA?
The operator installs the bracket upside down at assembly
Weld spatter is left on the bracket's mounting surface
A bracket wall specified too thin to carry the rated load
The torque gun drifts out of calibration between checks

A DFMEA covers failures that come from the design itself, such as an inadequate specified wall thickness. Assembly errors, weld spatter and tool calibration are manufacturing failures handled in a PFMEA.
std
VI.A
In a PFMEA, a failure mode has severity 8, occurrence 4 and detection 6. What is its risk priority number (RPN)?
RPN = S × O × D = 8 × 4 × 6 = 192. Adding the ratings (8 + 4 + 6 = 18) is a common error; the ratings are multiplied.
std
VI.A
A design team wants to lower the severity rating of a failure mode in its DFMEA. Which action can do that?
Change the design so the failure's effect is less serious
Add a final test that is more likely to catch the failure
Tighten process controls so the failure occurs less often
Train inspectors to recognize the failure more reliably

Severity rates the seriousness of the effect, so it can only drop when a design change makes the effect less serious. Better testing lowers the detection rating and tighter process control lowers occurrence, but neither changes severity.
std
VI.A
A seal leak keeps coming back. Each time, maintenance replaces the seal and the line restarts. What is missing from this approach to reducing risk?
A larger stock of spare seals at the line
A root cause analysis of why the seals fail
A faster seal replacement procedure for the crew
A record of each seal swap in the maintenance log
Replacing the seal fixes the symptom; only finding and removing the root cause stops the failure from returning. Faster swaps and more spares make the repair easier but leave the risk in place.
std
VI.A
A monthly report shows that 1,000 units started, 940 passed every test the first time, 45 passed after rework and 15 were scrapped. What is the first pass yield?
First pass yield counts only units that passed without rework or scrap: 940 ÷ 1,000 = 94.0%. Including reworked units gives (940 + 45) ÷ 1,000 = 98.5%, which hides the cost of rework.
std
VI.A
A weekly process monitoring report shows scrap on Line 3 rising from 1.2% to 2.8% over four weeks, while the other lines are flat. What should a quality technician do with this information?
Wait until Line 3 scrap passes the plant's yearly scrap target
Average all lines together, since the plant total is acceptable
Remove Line 3 from the report until its scrap returns to normal
Flag Line 3 as an emerging risk and find out what changed

Monitoring reports are useful for risk because they show a developing problem early, while it is still small and the cause is easier to find. Averaging lines together or waiting for a yearly target to be missed hides the signal.
std
VI.A
Customer complaints reveal a failure mode that is not listed in the product's PFMEA. What should happen to the PFMEA?
Add the failure mode and rate its severity, occurrence and detection
Leave the PFMEA unchanged, since it was approved at product launch
Note the complaint in the PFMEA header without any rating or action
Lower the detection ratings of all existing modes to show more caution

An FMEA is a living document, and complaints are a key input that should update it with the new failure mode and realistic ratings. Approval at launch does not freeze it when field evidence shows a gap.
std
VI.A
Over six months, 2,400 units of a pump were shipped and 18 were returned under warranty. What is the warranty return rate?
The return rate is 18 ÷ 2,400 = 0.0075, or 0.75%. Getting 7.5% or 0.075% comes from misplacing the decimal when converting to a percentage.

VI.A
Warranty returns for a product total 120: connector 54, seal 30, firmware 18, housing 12 and other 6. What share of returns do the top two categories account for?
Connector and seal together are 54 + 30 = 84 returns, and 84 ÷ 120 = 70%. Answering 45% counts only the connector category (54 ÷ 120).

VI.A
Which information does a control plan typically contain for each characteristic?
Root causes of past failures, with the people responsible for each one
Severity, occurrence and detection ratings, with an RPN for each failure mode
Process cycle times, staffing levels and the cost of each operation
Specification, measurement method, sample size and frequency, and reaction plan

A control plan lists what is controlled, to what requirement, how and how often it is checked, and what to do when it goes wrong. Severity, occurrence and detection ratings belong to the FMEA that feeds the control plan.
std
VI.A
A control plan entry says: "If a sample is out of tolerance, stop the machine, quarantine all parts since the last good check and notify the supervisor." What is this part of the control plan called?
The reaction plan
The control method
The sampling plan
The evaluation technique

The reaction plan states the actions to take when a check shows a nonconforming result or an out-of-control process. The control method describes how the characteristic is controlled, not what to do when it fails.

VI.B
A corrective action team starts by writing a problem statement. Which one is best?
Operators on press 4 are not careful enough when removing the housings
Since March 3, 14 of 600 press 4 housings have flash over 0.5 mm
Housing quality has gotten worse, and customers are unhappy about it
Press 4 needs a new mold because the old one makes bad housings
A good problem statement describes what, where, when and how much, without assuming a cause or a solution. The other statements blame people, are vague, or jump straight to a fix.
std
VI.B
A customer reports cracked fittings from lot 5512. What should be done first?
Start root cause analysis before taking any other action on the lot
Change the forming process to the setting the engineers think is best
Contain suspect stock at the plant, in transit and at the customer
Issue a corrective action request to the fitting material supplier

Containment protects the customer right away by isolating suspect product wherever it is, while the cause is still being found. Root cause work is essential but can take time, and suspect parts should not keep moving in the meantime.

VI.B
A press makes 80 parts per hour and is checked every hour. At the 10:00 check the part is out of tolerance; the last good check was at 8:30. How many parts, at minimum, should be held as suspect?
80 parts
40 parts
160 parts
120 parts
All parts made since the last good check are suspect: 1.5 hours × 80 parts per hour = 120 parts. Holding only 80 parts covers just the last hour, not the full time since the last good check.

VI.B
A containment sort of 1,200 parts finds 3 defective parts. What is the defect rate in parts per million (ppm)?
250 ppm
400 ppm
The rate is 3 ÷ 1,200 = 0.0025, and 0.0025 × 1,000,000 = 2,500 ppm. Answering 250 ppm comes from a decimal slip in converting the fraction.

VI.B
A drilling defect has recurred three times. Who should be assigned to determine its cause?
The quality technician working alone, because quality owns every corrective action
A small cross-functional team that includes people who know the drilling process
The operator on the shift when the defect last appeared, working by himself
The plant manager, because only senior managers can approve the final fix

Corrective action works best when named people with process knowledge and the right mix of skills are given clear responsibility for finding the cause. Leaving it to one person, or to whoever was on shift, misses knowledge and tends toward blame.

VI.B
A team finds that a worn locating pin causes misdrilled holes. Which is a permanent corrective action?
Sort all drilled parts 100% until further notice from engineering
Retrain the operator who was running the drill when it happened
Fit a hardened pin and add pin wear checks to preventive maintenance
Post a caution sign at the drill reminding operators to check every hole
A permanent action removes the root cause, here pin wear, and keeps it from returning. Sorting is containment, and retraining or signs do not address a worn pin.

VI.B
Which of these is an interim action rather than a permanent corrective action?
Redesigning the fixture so the part cannot be loaded backward
Changing the drawing tolerance after a capability study
Replacing the feeder that caused the jams with a new design
100% inspection of outgoing parts until the fix is in place

Interim (containment) actions protect the customer while the cause is being removed, and 100% inspection is a typical example. The other options change the design, the specification or the equipment to remove the cause permanently.

VI.B
A supervisor reports that a corrective action is done: a new fixture, a revised work instruction and operator training. How should the quality technician verify implementation?
Go to the process and see the fixture, instruction and training records
Accept the supervisor's report, since supervisors are responsible for the area
Check that customer complaints have stopped over the next three months
Ask the operators whether they think the problem is now fixed
Verifying implementation means seeing objective evidence that each planned action was actually carried out. Tracking complaints over time checks effectiveness, which is a separate later step.

VI.B
Before a corrective action, 64 of 2,000 parts were defective. After it, 12 of 2,000 are defective. By what percentage did the defect rate fall?
The rate fell from 3.2% to 0.6%, and (3.2 − 0.6) ÷ 3.2 = 81.25%. Answering 2.6% gives the drop in percentage points, not the relative reduction.
std
VI.B
Two weeks after a fix, no defects have been seen. The process runs one lot a month, and before the fix the defect appeared about once every quarter. What is the best conclusion?
The action is effective, since no defects have been seen since the fix
The action failed, since too little data exists to prove it worked
It is too soon to judge effectiveness; keep monitoring over more lots
The corrective action can be closed now and reopened if defects return

Effectiveness has to be shown over a period long enough that the problem would have shown up if it were still present. Two weeks with no defects tells little about a defect that appeared about once a quarter.
std
VI.B
What is the difference between verifying implementation and confirming effectiveness of a corrective action?
Implementation is done by the customer; effectiveness is done by the supplier
Implementation reviews root cause; effectiveness reviews the containment results
Implementation happens at launch; effectiveness is needed only after a complaint
Implementation checks the action was done; effectiveness checks the problem is gone

Verification shows the planned actions are in place, while validation of effectiveness shows the problem has not recurred over time. A correctly installed fix can still fail to work, which is why both steps are needed.
std
VI.C
Which of these is a preventive action rather than a corrective action?
Adding a sensor that stops a press before a fault the FMEA rated likely
Reworking a lot of parts that failed final inspection for a missing hole
Replacing a cracked die after it produced a run of nonconforming parts
Retraining an inspector after a customer returned a shipment of parts

Preventive action addresses a potential problem before it occurs, here a fault the FMEA identified as likely. The other options respond to problems that have already happened, which is correction or corrective action.
std
VI.C
A team is launching a new assembly line and wants to decide which potential failures to address before production starts. Which technique fits best?
A histogram of last month's shipping weights from the existing line
A PFMEA rating each failure mode's severity, occurrence and detection
A Pareto chart of the new line's customer complaints from last year
A scatter diagram of overtime hours against output on the old line

A PFMEA is designed to identify and rank potential failures before they happen, which is what preventive action needs. A new line has no complaint history to chart, and the other data says little about how the new process could fail.
std
VI.C

A control chart shows the process average drifting steadily toward the upper limit, with no point yet outside the limits and no defects found. The team acts on the cause now. What kind of action is this?
Corrective action for a nonconformity
Containment of suspect product
Preventive action based on trend data
Correction of a defect
Acting on a trend before any nonconformity occurs is preventive, because it deals with a potential problem. Corrective action responds to a nonconformity that has already happened, and none has here.
std
VI.C
A preventive action is opened to reduce the risk of mixed parts at a packing station. Who should be responsible for carrying out the process improvement?
The auditor who first noticed the risk during an internal audit
The customer, because mixed parts would affect the customer most
Whoever has the lightest workload in the quality department that week
The packing process owner, helped by those who will make the change

Responsibility for improving a process belongs with the people who own and run it, with help from those who will build or change things. Auditors report risk but do not own fixes, since that would compromise their independence.
std
VI.C
A part can be loaded into a fixture backward, which produces a scrap part. Which is the strongest mistake-proofing solution?
A locating pin that lets the part seat only in the correct orientation
A warning label on the fixture showing the correct direction for loading
An added inspection after the operation to catch backward-loaded parts
Retraining operators on the loading direction during each shift start
A physical feature that prevents the error from being made is the strongest form of mistake-proofing. Inspection detects the error after the fact, and labels or training rely on people remembering.
std
VI.C
A sensor stops an assembly machine before the cycle starts if a washer is missing. What type of mistake-proofing device is this?
A warning device that alerts the operator but lets the cycle run
A control device that keeps the error from producing a defect
A detection check that sorts out defects after they are made
A visual aid that shows the operator where the washer goes
Stopping the machine before the cycle runs is a control-type device, the stronger of the two main types. A warning-type device only signals the problem and relies on the operator to respond.
std
VI.C
A review finds operators often skip a purge step after material changes because the work instruction lists it on page 4, after unrelated notes. Which preventive action fits best?
Remind operators about the purge step at the next shift meeting
Add the purge step to the plant newsletter as a safety reminder
Move the purge step into sequence in the instruction, with a sign-off
Increase final inspection on the first lot after each material change

The weakness is in the procedure itself, so changing the procedure removes the cause for every operator and shift. Reminders fade over time, and added inspection only catches problems after they occur.
std
VI.C
Before launching a new product, a team reviews problems recorded on similar past launches and builds those fixes into the new design and process. What is the team doing?
Performing containment
Running a product audit
Taking corrective action
Applying lessons learned

Using recorded experience from past projects to avoid repeating their problems is applying lessons learned, a key preventive tool. Corrective action addresses a nonconformity that has already occurred on this product, and none has yet.
std
VI.C
On Line A, cracked welds are traced to a wrong wire feed setting. Lines B and C use the same robot model and the same setting but have had no cracks so far. What does read across call for?
Check Lines B and C for the same risk and apply the fix where needed
Wait for cracked welds on Lines B and C before changing their setting
Close the action, since only Line A has produced any cracked welds
Shut down Lines B and C until a new robot model can be installed

Read across extends a lesson or fix from one problem to similar products, processes or sites that share the same risk, before they fail. Waiting for the same failure to appear elsewhere turns a preventable problem into a corrective action.

VI.C
Before a mistake-proofing device was added, a station had 14 misassemblies in 7,000 units. What was the rate in parts per million (ppm)?
200 ppm
500 ppm
The rate is 14 ÷ 7,000 = 0.002, and 0.002 × 1,000,000 = 2,000 ppm. Answering 200 ppm results from a decimal slip in the conversion.
std
VI.C
Six months after a mistake-proofing sensor was installed, what is the best way to verify that the preventive action is effective?
Confirm the purchase order for the sensor was approved and paid on time
Ask the operators whether they like working with the new sensor each day
Review the failure data and confirm the sensor still stops bad parts
Check that the sensor appears on the plant's list of installed equipment

Effectiveness is shown by evidence that the potential failure has not occurred, plus routine checks that the device still functions, for example with a known bad part. Paperwork and opinions show the device exists, not that it prevents the failure.
